2.6.2.1.2. Class Condition

         The class condition determines whether the operand is numeric, that is, consists entirely
         of the characters ΓÇ£0ΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£1ΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£2ΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£3ΓÇ¥, ..., ΓÇ£9ΓÇ¥, with or without the operational sign,
         alphabetic, that is, consists entirely of the characters ΓÇ£AΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£BΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£CΓÇ¥, ..., ΓÇ£aΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£bΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£cΓÇ¥,
         ..., ΓÇ£zΓÇ¥,space; or CLASSΓÇôNAME, that is, consists entirely of the characters specified in
         the CLASSΓÇôNAME clause of the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES paragraph. The general format for
         the class condition is as follows:
                                   NUMERIC
           identifier IS [ NOT ]   ALPHABETIC
                                   CLASS-NAME mnemonic-name

         The usage of the operand being tested must be described as display. The USAGE of the
         operand may also be COMPΓÇô3, when IBM OS/360 allocation rules apply (see Table 15-2).
         When used, ΓÇ£NOTΓÇ¥ and the next key word specify one class condition that defines the
         class test to be executed for truth value; for example, ΓÇ£NOT NUMERICΓÇ¥ is a truth test for
         determining that an operand is nonnumeric.

         The NUMERIC test cannot be used with an item whose data description describes the
         item as alphabetic or as a group item composed of elementary items whose data
         description indicates the presence of operational signs. If the data description of the
         item being tested does not indicate the presence of an operational sign, the item being
         tested is determined to be numeric only if the contents are numeric and an operational
         sign is not present. If the data description of the item does indicate the presence of an
         operational sign, the item being tested is determined to be numeric only if the contents
         are numeric and a valid operational sign is present. Valid operational signs for data items
         described with the SIGN IS SEPARATE clause are the standard data format characters,
         ΓÇ£+ΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£-ΓÇ¥. See Table 2-1 for what constitutes valid signs for data items not described
         with the SIGN IS SEPARATE clause.

         The ALPHABETIC test cannot be used with an item whose data description describes the
         item as numeric. The item being tested is determined to be alphabetic only if the contents
         consist of any combination of the alphabetic characters ΓÇ£AΓÇ¥ through ΓÇ£ZΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£aΓÇ¥ through ΓÇ£zΓÇ¥,
         and the space.

         The CLASSΓÇôNAME test allows specification of an alphabetic, numeric, or
         SOURCE-ALPHABET subset.

2.6.2.1.3. Condition-Name Condition (Conditional Variable)

          In a condition-name condition, a conditional variable is tested to determine whether or
          not its value is equal to one of the values associated with a condition-name. The general
          format for the condition-name condition is:
           condition-name

          If the condition-name is associated with a range or ranges of values, then the conditional
          variable is tested to determine whether or not its value falls in this range, including the
          end values.

          The rules for comparing a conditional variable with a condition-name value are the same
          as those specified for relation conditions.

          The result of the test is true if one of the values corresponding to the condition-name
          equals the value of its associated conditional variable.

          For example, the data description of a particular conditional variable might appear as:
             02 MARITAL-STATUS PICTURE IS 9.
                  88 SINGLE VALUE IS 1.
                  88 MARRIED VALUE IS 2.
                  88 DIVORCED VALUE IS 3.
                  88 WIDOWED VALUE IS 4.
                  88 EVER-MARRIED VALUE 2 THRU 4.

          Using an IF statement, the test to determine marital status may appear as:
             IF MARRIED . . .

          which is equivalent to:
             IF MARITAL-STATUS IS EQUAL TO 2

          Again, as in the relational condition, NOT is used to specify the opposite of what the
          condition-name test would normally specify. So, for example:
             IF NOT SINGLE . . .

          is equivalent to:
             IF MARITAL-STATUS IS NOT EQUAL TO 1




2ΓÇô56                                                                                 7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                            Nucleus




         The same situation could be checked by writing:
            IF EVER-MARRIED . . .

         which is equivalent to:
            IF MARITAL-STATUS NOT < 2 AND
               MARITAL-STATUS NOT > 4 . . .

         When a single condition-name is associated with a list of values or ranges of values, a
         programmer may express what is equivalent to rather complex compound relationals in a
         simple condition-name condition.

         For example, the code names for various bolts in inventory might be:
            03 PART-NUMBER PIC X(5).
              88 BOLT VALUE IS ΓÇ£AA000ΓÇ¥ THRU
                ΓÇ£AA999ΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£AX010ΓÇ¥ THRU ΓÇ£AZ999ΓÇ¥,
                  ΓÇ£P1000ΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£P1010ΓÇ¥.

         Using the IF statement to determine whether the part is a bolt, a programmer can write:
            IF BOLT GO TO IS-BOLT.

         which is equivalent to writing:
            IF PART-NUMBER NOT < ΓÇ£AA000ΓÇ¥ AND
                   PART-NUMBER NOT > ΓÇ£AA999ΓÇ¥ OR
                   PART-NUMBER NOT > ΓÇ£AX010ΓÇ¥ AND
                   PART-NUMBER NOT > ΓÇ£AZ999ΓÇ¥ OR
                   PART-NUMBER = ΓÇ£P1000ΓÇ¥ OR ΓÇ£P1010ΓÇ¥
                   GO TO IS-BOLT .

2.6.2.1.4. SwitchΓÇôStatus Condition

         A switch-status condition determines the ΓÇ£onΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£offΓÇ¥ status of an implementor-
         defined switch. The implementor-name and the ΓÇ£onΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£offΓÇ¥ value associated with the
         condition must be named in the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES paragraph of the Environment
         Division. The general format for the switch-status condition is:
           condition-name

         The result of the test is true if the switch is set to the specified position corresponding to
         condition-name.

         The implementor-names SWITCHΓÇô13, SWITCHΓÇô14, . . ., SWITCHΓÇô24 correspond to the
         bits in the last third of the condition word set by the SET mnemonic-name verb. Thus,
         SWITCHΓÇô13 is bit 24, SWITCHΓÇô14 is bit 25, . . ., SWITCHΓÇô24 is bit 35. The switch-status
         condition ON checks for a 1 in the appropriate bit, OFF checks for a 0.

         The implementor-names SWITCHΓÇô1, SWITCHΓÇô2, . . ., SWITCHΓÇô12 correspond to the bits
         in the middle or second third of the condition word set by the @SETC command
         statement. Thus, SWITCHΓÇô1 is bit 12, SWITCHΓÇô2 is bit 13, . . ., SWITCHΓÇô12 is bit 23.
         The switch-status condition ON checks for a 1 in the appropriate bit, OFF checks for a 0.

             @SETC 153/T2

2.6.2.1.5. Sign Condition

          The sign condition determines whether or not the algebraic value of an arithmetic
          expression is less than, greater than, or equal to zero. The general format for a sign
          condition follows.

                                                    POSITIVE
            arithmetic-expression   IS [ NOT ]      NEGATIVE
                                                    ZERO

          When used, ΓÇ£NOTΓÇ¥ and the next key word specify one sign condition that defines the
          algebraic test to be executed for truth value; for example, ΓÇ£NOT ZEROΓÇ¥ is a truth test for
          a nonzero (positive or negative) value. An operand is positive if its value is greater than
          zero, negative if its value is less than zero, and zero if its value is equal to zero. The zero
          test will be true for any numeric item containing a zero even if the field contains a
          positive or negative operational sign. The arithmetic expression must contain at least
          one reference to a variable.

         Any condition that can be expressed in a numeric status test may also be expressed by a
         relational expression. For example:
            A + B + C IS POSITIVE

         may also be expressed in a relational expression as:
            A + B + C IS GREATER THAN 0


2.6.2.2. Complex Conditions

         A complex condition is formed by combining simple conditions, combined conditions
         and/or complex conditions with logical connectors (logical operators ΓÇ£ANDΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£ORΓÇ¥),
         or negating these conditions with logical negation (the logical operator ΓÇ£NOTΓÇ¥). The
         truth value of a complex condition, whether parenthesized or not, is that truth value
         which results from the interaction of all the stated logical operators on the individual
         truth values of simple conditions, or the intermediate truth values of conditions logically
         connected or logically negated.

         The logical operators and their meanings are:


            Logical Operator                                     Meaning
                                Logical conjunction; the truth value is ΓÇ£trueΓÇ¥ if both of the conjoined
                  AND
                                conditions are true; ΓÇ£falseΓÇ¥ if one or both of the conjoined conditions is
                                false
                                Logical inclusive OR; the truth value is ΓÇ£trueΓÇ¥ if one or both of the
                  OR
                                included conditions is true; ΓÇ£falseΓÇ¥ if both included conditions are false
                                Logical negation or reversal of truth value; the truth value is ΓÇ£trueΓÇ¥ if
                  NOT
                                the condition is false; ΓÇ£falseΓÇ¥ if the condition is true.


         The logical operators must be preceded by a space and followed by a space.

2.6.2.2.1. Negated Simple Conditions

         A simple condition (see 2.6.2.1) is negated through the use of the logical operator
         ΓÇ£NOTΓÇ¥. The negated simple condition affects the opposite truth value for a simple
         condition. Thus the truth value of a negated simple condition is ΓÇ£trueΓÇ¥ if and only if the
         truth value of the simple condition is ΓÇ£falseΓÇ¥; the truth value of a negated simple
         condition is ΓÇ£falseΓÇ¥ if and only if the truth value of the simple condition is ΓÇ£trueΓÇ¥. The
         inclusion in parentheses of a negated simple condition does not change the truth value.

         The general format for a negated simple condition is:
             NOT simple-condition

             A = B

          and:
             NOT A = B

          will have the effect that if A = B is true, NOT A = B will be false, and vice versa.

2.6.2.2.2. Combined and Negated Combined Conditions

          A combined condition results from connecting conditions with one of the logical
          operators ΓÇ£ANDΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£ORΓÇ¥. The general format of a combined condition is:

                           AND
           condition                condition      ...
                           OR

          where condition may be:

          1. A simple condition, or
          2. A negated simple condition, or
          3. A combined condition, or
          4. A negated combined condition, in other words, the ΓÇ£NOTΓÇ¥ logical operator followed
             by a combined condition enclosed within parentheses, or
          5. Combinations of 1 through 4, specified according to the rules summarized in
             Table 2-9.

          Although parentheses need never be used when either ΓÇ£ANDΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£ORΓÇ¥ (but not both) is
          used exclusively in a combined condition, parentheses may be used to effect a final truth
          value when a mixture of ΓÇ£ANDΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£ORΓÇ¥, and ΓÇ£NOTΓÇ¥ is used. (See Table 2-9 and the
          condition evaluation rules in 2.6.2.4.)

         relation condition except the first may be abbreviated by:

         2. The omission of the subject and relational operator of the relation condition.

2.6.2.4. Condition Evaluation Rules

         Parentheses may be used to specify the order in which individual conditions of complex
         conditions are to be evaluated when it is necessary to depart from the implied evaluation
         precedence. Conditions within parentheses are evaluated first and, within nested
         parentheses, evaluation proceeds from the least inclusive condition to the most inclusive
         condition. When parentheses are not used, or parenthesized conditions are at the same
         level of inclusiveness, the following hierarchical order of logical evaluation is implied until
         the final truth value is determined:

         1. Values are established for arithmetic expressions. (See 2.6.1.3.)
         2. Truth values for simple conditions are established in the following order:
                 relation (following the expansion of any abbreviated relation condition)
                 class
                 condition-name
                 switch-status
                 sign
         3. Truth values for negated simple conditions are established
         4. Truth values for combined conditions are established:
                 ΓÇ£ANDΓÇ¥ logical operators, followed by
                 ΓÇ£ORΓÇ¥ logical operators.
         5. Truth values for negated combined conditions are established.
         6. When the sequence of evaluation is not completely specified by parentheses, the
            order of evaluation of consecutive operations of the same hierarchical level is from
            left to right.

2.6.3. Common Phrases and General Rules for Statement Formats
         In the statement descriptions that follow, several phrases appear frequently: the
         ROUNDED phrase, the SIZE ERROR phrase, and the CORRESPONDING phrase.

         In the discussion which follows, a resultant-identifier is that identifier associated with a
         result of an arithmetic operation.

2.6.3.1. The ROUNDED Phrase
         If, after decimal point alignment, the number of places in the fraction of the result of an
         arithmetic operation is greater than the number of places provided for the fraction of the
         resultant-identifier, truncation is relative to the size provided for the resultant-identifier.
         When rounding is requested, the absolute value of the resultant-identifier is increased by
         one whenever the most significant digit of the excess is greater than or equal to five.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                      2ΓÇô63
Nucleus




          When the low-order integer positions in a resultant-identifier are represented by the
          character ΓÇ£PΓÇ¥ in the picture for that resultant-identifier, rounding or truncation occurs
          relative to the rightmost integer position for which storage is allocated.

          For example, if addition operands are:

             02 A PIC 99V99 VALUE 10.51.
             02 B PIC 99V9(3) VALUE 96.299.
             02 C PIC 999.
             02 D PIC 999V9(3).
             02 E PIC 999V9.
             02 F PIC 999P.

          and the statements executed are:

             ADD A , B GIVING C ROUNDED.
             ADD A , B GIVING C.
             ADD A , B GIVING D ROUNDED.
             ADD A , B GIVING D.
             ADD A , B GIVING E ROUNDED.
             ADD A , B GIVING F ROUNDED.

          the results will be C = 107, C = 106, D = 106.809, D = 106.809, E = 106.8, and F = 011,
          respectively.

2.6.3.2. The SIZE ERROR Phrase
          If, after decimal point alignment, the absolute value of a result exceeds the largest value
          that can be contained in the associated resultant-identifier, a size error condition exists.
          Division by zero always causes a size error condition. The size error condition applies
          only to the final results of an arithmetic operation and does not apply to intermediate
          results, except in the MULTIPLY and DIVIDE statements, in which case the size error
          condition applies to the intermediate results as well. If the ROUNDED phrase is
          specified, rounding takes place before checking for size error. When such a size error
          condition occurs, the subsequent action depends on whether or not the SIZE ERROR
          phrase is specified.
          1. If the SIZE ERROR phrase is not specified and a size error condition occurs, the
             value of those resultant-identifiers affected is undefined. Values of resultant-
             identifiers for which no size error condition occurs are unaffected by size errors that
             occur for other resultant-identifiers during execution of this operation.
          2. If the SIZE ERROR phrase is specified and a size error condition occurs, then the
             values of resultant-identifiers affected by the size errors are not altered. Values of
             resultant-identifiers for which no size error condition occurs are unaffected by size
             errors that occur for other resultant-identifiers during execution of this operation.
             After completion of the execution of this operation, the imperative statement in the
             SIZE ERROR phrase is executed.




2ΓÇô64                                                                                   7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                             Nucleus




             For the ADD statement with the CORRESPONDING phrase and the SUBTRACT
             statement with the CORRESPONDING phrase, if any of the individual operations
             produces a size error condition, the imperative statement in the SIZE ERROR phrase
             is not executed until all of the individual additions or subtractions are completed.

         For example, if data fields are defined as:
            02 A PIC 99V9.
            02 B PIC 99V9.
            02 C PIC 999V9.

         the statement ADD A, B GIVING C will not produce a size error condition if A and B do
         indeed contain numeric values. If, however, a sum is being developed such as:
            ADD A TO B.

         a size error condition could occur.

         Note: For an item with the USAGE COMPUTATIONAL clause, the test for SIZE ERROR
         condition uses the maximum decimal value according to the original PICTURE regardless
         of bit size. For example:
           A1 PIC 99 COMP.

         A1 is allocated 9 bits. A value of 100 can fit in 9 bits but it would cause a size error
         condition.

         For floating-point arithmetic a size error condition will occur if a hardware floating-point
         interrupt occurs or if a floating-point intermediate result cannot be contained in the
         designated receiving field. Exponentiation is accomplished in floating-point arithmetic. If
         a floating-point interrupt occurs during an exponentiation, it is treated as a run-time error
         condition rather than a size error condition and the execution is terminated. Termination
         occurs if:

         1. The result has a zero characteristic and a mantissa less than or equal to zero.
         2. The result has a characteristic less than zero and a nonintegral mantissa.
         3. The result is such that the mantissa times the LN of the characteristics is greater
            than 709.089.

            and d2.
         2. At least one of the data items is an elementary data item in the case of a MOVE
            statement with the CORRESPONDING phrase; and both of the data items are
            elementary numeric data items in the case of the ADD statement with the
            CORRESPONDING phrase or the SUBTRACT statement with the CORRESPONDING

2.6.3.4. The Arithmetic Statements
         The arithmetic statements are the ADD, COMPUTE, DIVIDE, MULTIPLY, and
         SUBTRACT statements. They have several common features.
         1. The data descriptions of the operands need not be the same. Any necessary
            conversion and decimal point alignment is supplied throughout the calculation.
         2. The maximum size of each operand is 18 decimal digits. The composite of
            operands, which is a hypothetical data item resulting from the superimposition of
            specified operands in a statement aligned on their decimal points (see 2.6.5 for the
            ADD statement, 2.6.9 for the DIVIDE statement, 2.6.15 for the MULTIPLY
            statement, and 2.6.20 for the SUBTRACT statement) must not contain more than 18
            decimal digits.

2.6.3.5. Overlapping Operands
         When a sending and a receiving item in an arithmetic statement or an INSPECT, MOVE,
         SET, STRING, or UNSTRING statement share a part of their storage areas, the result of
         the execution of such a statement is undefined.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                2ΓÇô67
Nucleus




2.6.3.6. Multiple Results in Arithmetic Statements

          The ADD, COMPUTE, DIVIDE, MULTIPLY, and SUBTRACT statements may have
          multiple results. Such statements behave as though they had been written in the
          following way:
          1. A statement which performs all arithmetic necessary to arrive at the result to be
             stored in the receiving items, and stores that result in a temporary storage location.
          2. A sequence of statements transferring or combining the value of this temporary
             location with a single result. These statements are considered to be written in the
             same leftΓÇôtoΓÇôright sequence that the multiple results are listed.
          The result of the statement:
            ADD a, b, c TO c, d (c), e

          is equivalent to:
            ADD a, b, c GIVING temp
            ADD temp TO c
            ADD temp TO d (c)
            ADD temp TO e

          where temp is an intermediate result item provided by the compiler.

2.6.3.7. Arithmetic Intermediate Results

          Whenever an arithmetic expression is resolved or an arithmetic statement is executed,
          there is an intermediate result which has characteristics determined by the
          characteristics of the operands and in some cases by the characteristics of the eventual
          resultant field.

          These characteristics are mode (USAGE of the items), sign (the presence or absence of
          an operational sign), size (the number of digit positions which the items can contain), and
          scaling (the position of the assumed decimal point). The characteristics determine what
          values an item may assume and how the calculations involving the item are made.

          When the characteristics and the values are not compatible, either a truncation or a size
          error condition exists. Truncation conditions occur when the value, after decimal
          alignment, contains excessive low order digits. Size error conditions occur when the
          value, after decimal alignment, contains excessive high order digits.

          The statements ADD, SUBTRACT, MULTIPLY, DIVIDE, and COMPUTE allow a
          programmer to correct or compensate when either situation occurs by using the
          ROUNDED and SIZE ERROR options.

          Arithmetic expressions in the PERFORM, IF, and SEARCH statements, however, do not
          provide alternate actions and can produce either left or right truncation of the
          expressionΓÇÖs resolved value.




2ΓÇô68                                                                                 7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                            Nucleus




         The characteristics of intermediate results, regardless of the statement type, are
         described in the following paragraphs.

         The compiler deals with arithmetic operations separately for each pair of operands. For
         example, in the statement:
            COMPUTE A = B + C - D

         B and C determine the characteristics of the first intermediate result of the addition. The
         sum and the field D determine the characteristics of the final intermediate result. Then
         the characteristics of A are used to determine the correct way to move the result to the
         final receiving field. Thus, the preceding example is equivalent to:
            COMPUTE temp1 = B + C

            COMPUTE temp2 = temp1 - D

            MOVE temp2 TO A

         and each value is aligned and each result is computed based solely on the characteristics
         of the operands involved in the intermediate calculation. Only for division are the
         characteristics of scale and size of the receiving field used to determine the
         characteristics of the intermediate result.

         Arithmetic results are calculated in one of three ways. The method is determined by the
         USAGE of the fields involved and the operator specified. The three modes of calculation
         are decimal, binary, and floating-point.

         Decimal arithmetic is addition or subtraction which is performed directly on the
         characters composing the operands:
         D1          scaling positions in operand 1
         D2          scaling positions in operand 2
         DMAX        greater of D1 and D2
         NB          number of bytes per word (4)
         SB1         starting byte of operand 1 (0-3)
         SB2         starting byte of operand 2 (0-3)
         SZ1         size of operand 1 in bytes
         SZ2         size of operand 2 in bytes
         ///         remainder from division




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                  2ΓÇô69
Nucleus




          Decimal arithmetic is done only if all of the following conditions are met:

          1. SZ1 + SB1 Γëñ 3 * NB
          2. SZ2 + SB2 Γëñ 3 * NB
          3. (DMAX - D1 + SB1) /// NB + SZ1 Γëñ 3 * NB
          4. (DMAX - D2 + SB2) /// NB + SZ2 Γëñ 3 * NB
          5. Both operands must be array synchronized (subscripted items must always begin at
             the same byte number)
          6. Both operands must be DISPLAY.

          If either or both operands of any calculation are floating-point (COMPUTATIONALΓÇô1 or
          COMPUTATIONALΓÇô2) or if exponentiation is required, calculations are performed in
          floating-point with any nonfloating-point items being converted to floating-point format.

          In all other cases calculations are performed in binary and operands which are not in
          binary format will be converted to binary prior to calculations.

          Like scaling and decimal alignment, the mode of calculation is determined separately for
          each intermediate calculation. For example, assuming:
             A, B, E, and X are DISPLAY
             C, D, and F are COMP

          the statement:
             COMPUTE X = A + B - C ** D/(E - F)
          will be resolved as follows:
          1. Decimal mode A + B = temp1
          2. Convert C and D to floating point
          3. Floating mode C ** D = temp2
          4. Convert E to binary
          5. Binary mode E - F = temp3
          6. Convert temp3 to floating point
          7. Floating mode temp2/temp3 = temp4
          8. Convert temp1 to floating point
          9. Floating mode temp1 - temp4 = temp5
          10. Convert temp5 to DISPLAY and store in X
          An understanding of the different calculation modes is important when determining the
          size of intermediate results. When calculations are performed in decimal mode no more
          than 18 digits of significance is possible and if a calculation would result in exceeding the
          maximum low order characters are dropped without rounding.




2ΓÇô70                                                                                    7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                            Nucleus




         However, since the OS 2200 System is intrinsically a binary rather than a decimal
         computer, binary fields can actually contain more digits of precision than is indicated by
         their PICTURE clause. For example, an S9(10) COMPUTATIONAL item is allocated as a
         36-bit field. Those 36 bits can contain an absolute value up to 34,359,738,367.

         If, during intermediate calculations, such a field contains a value greater than
         9,999,999,999 but less than 235, the full value is used in subsequent intermediate
         calculations.

         Similarly, a full two-word binary number can contain 21 digits of significance. Therefore,
         intermediate results of binary calculations are held and used in subsequent intermediate
         calculations as maximum 21-digit capacity items. During calculations involving binary
         items the compiler will assure that intermediate results are sufficiently large, up to 21
         digits, to retain precision and significance.

         Floating-point intermediate results are maintained as either single or double precision
         floating-point items, whichever will suffice to contain the calculated results. The capacity
         of floating-point data items is sufficiently large for most applications. Single precision
         floating-point (COMPΓÇô1) can represent a binary characteristic (exponent) of 127 through -
         128 applied to a mantissa (base) of ┬▒227 - 1.

         COMPUTATIONALΓÇô2 fields and double precision floating-point intermediate results can
         represent a binary characteristic of 1023 through -1024 applied to a mantissa of ┬▒260 - 1.
         Floating-point calculations which result in invalid floating-point values are explained in
         2.6.3.2, the SIZE ERROR phrase.

         A user should be aware of difficulties which may arise because of floating point
         arithmetic and take corrective action if necessary. When a floating-point intermediate
         result is converted and stored in a binary or character field, the result may be imprecise
         in the least significant position. For example, 4 * * 3 might result in 63.999... instead of
         64.000... . Therefore, it is advisable, if a process requires a precise answer, to specify
         ROUNDED for nonfloating-point receiving fields when floating-point arithmetic is done.

          The algorithms for calculating the size and assumed decimal point of nonfloating-point

          their meanings are:

          N1 and N2

          N3
                is the number of integer places in the intermediate sum, difference, product, or
                 quotient.

          N4
                is the number of integer places in the remainder of a division operation.

          D1,D2,D3, and D4
                 are the number of scaling positions in the field. If a field has scale n, this means that
                its integer value is implicitly multiplied by 10ΓÇôn whenever the field is used. For a
               decimal field, having scale n is equivalent to having n decimal places following an
               assumed decimal point.

          NR and DR
               are the number of integer and decimal digits in the ultimate receiving field. If there
               are multiple receiving fields, the largest NR and the largest DR is used. In this case,
               NR and DR do not necessarily derive from the same receiving field. When the
               receiving field is a floating point item, NR is assumed to be 18 and DR is 0.

          For division, operand1 is the dividend and operand2 is the divisor. For other operations,
          the use of the operands is not differentiated when determining the size of an
          intermediate result.

2.6.3.8. Incompatible Data
         Except for the class condition (see 2.6.2.1.2) when the contents of a data item are
         referenced in the Procedure Division and the contents of that data item are not
         compatible with the class specified for that data item by its PICTURE clause, the result
         of such a reference is undefined.

2.6.4. The ACCEPT Statement
2.6.4.1. Function
          The ACCEPT statement causes low volume data to be made available to the specified
          data item.

2.6.4.2. General Format
          Format 1
          ACCEPT identifier   [ FROM mnemonic-name ]

          Format 2

                                       DATE [YYYYMMDD]
           ACCEPT identifier FROM      DAY [YYYYDDD]
                                       TIME
                                       DATE-TIME [MMDDYYYY]


2.6.4.3. Syntax Rules
          1. The mnemonic-name in Format 1 must also be specified in the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES
             paragraph of the Environment Division and must be associated with the
             implementor-names CARDΓÇôREADER or CONSOLE.

2.6.4.4. General Rules

          Format 1
          1. The ACCEPT statement causes the transfer of data from the hardware device. This
             data replaces the contents of the data item named by the identifier.
             When the device is the CONSOLE, programs executing in batch mode will accept
             data from the operatorΓÇÖs console. In batch mode CARDΓÇôREADER specifies the
             program card file device. For programs executing in demand mode, CONSOLE and
             CARDΓÇôREADER both specify the demand terminal.

             The execution of an ACCEPT statement specifying the operatorΓÇÖs terminal or
             demand terminal will not permit execution of subsequent instructions until a
             response is made. It is therefore usually advisable to precede such ACCEPT
             statements with a DISPLAY to the console or terminal explaining what data is
             desired.

             The presence of the B option on the @XQT statement will cause a program to
             operate in batch mode for purposes of the ACCEPT statement.




2ΓÇô80                                                                             7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                             Nucleus




         2. The amount of data which can be handled in a single transfer differs with the type of
            device.

            Specified Device
            Implementor-Name         Size of a Single Data Transfer
            CARDΓÇôREADER              80 characters for programs executing in batch mode
                                     72 characters for programs executing in demand mode
            CONSOLE                  50 characters for programs executing in batch mode
                                     72 characters for programs executing in demand mode



         3. If a hardware device can transfer data of the same size as the receiving data item,
            the transferred data is stored in the receiving data item.
         4. If a hardware device cannot transfer data of the same size as the receiving data item,
            and the receiving item is alphanumeric, then:
             a.   If the size of the receiving data item (or of the portion of the receiving data item
                  not yet currently occupied by transferred data) exceeds the size of the
                  transferred data, the transferred data is stored aligned to the left in the receiving
                  data item (or the portion of the receiving data item not yet occupied), and
                  additional data is requested. In Level 1, only one transfer of data is provided.
             b. If the size of the transferred data exceeds the size of the receiving data item (or
                of the portion of the receiving data item not yet occupied by transferred data),
                only the leftmost characters of the transferred data are stored in the receiving
                data item (or in the portion remaining). The remaining characters of the
                transferred data which do not fit into the receiving data item are ignored.
         5. For a numeric receiving field: data preceding a space in the field is assumed to be an
            integer value which is converted as necessary, aligned to the right and zero-filled,
            and treated as an integer for subsequent transfer to the receiving field. A signed
            data item should be entered as a sign is trailing (not separate) item.
         6. The acceptance devices all use character data representation. Thus, input is in ASCII
            characters. When the receiving field has a usage of other than ASCII the data is
            converted, then placed in the receiving area.

             The actual value of the accepted data is not examined. Thus, coding a value in the
             form of a floating point constant will be treated simply as a character string which
             happens to have the character ΓÇ£EΓÇ¥ embedded in it.
         7. If the FROM phrase is not given, the CONSOLE is assumed to be the input device.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                     2ΓÇô81
Nucleus




          Format 2

          8. The ACCEPT statement causes the information requested to be transferred to the
             data item specified by identifier according to the rules of the MOVE statement.
             DATE, DAY, and TIME are conceptual data items and, therefore, are not described in
             the COBOL program.
          9. DATE, without the YYYYMMDD phrase, is composed of the data elements year of
             century, month of year, and day of month. The sequence of the data element codes
             shall be from high order to low order (left to right), year of century, month of year,
             and day of month. Therefore, July 1, 1968 would be expressed as 680701. DATE,
             without the YYYYMMDD phrase, when accessed by a COBOL program, behaves as
             if it had been described in the COBOL program as an unsigned elementary numeric
             integer data item six digits in length.

              DATE with the YYYYMMDD phrase is composed of the data elements year including
              century, month of year, day of month. The sequence of the data element codes shall
              be from high order to low order (left to right), year including century, month of year
              and day of month. Therefore, July 1, 1968 would be expressed as 19680701. DATE
              with the YYYYMMDD phrase when accessed by a COBOL program, behaves as if it
              had been described in a COBOL program as an unsigned elementary numeric integer
              data item eight digits in length.

          10. DAY without the YYYYDDD phrase is composed of the data elements year of
              century and day of year. The sequence of the data element codes shall be from high
              order to low order (left to right), year of century, and day of year. Therefore, July 1,
              1968 would be expressed as 1968183. DAY without the YYYYDDD phrase, when
              accessed by a COBOL program, behaves as if it had been described in a COBOL
              program as an unsigned elementary numeric integer data item five digits in length.

              DAY with the YYYYDDD phrase is composed of the data elements year including
              century and day of year. The sequence of the data element codes shall be from high
              order to low order (left to right), year including century and day of year. Therefore,
              July 1, 1968 would be expressed as 1968183. DAY with the YYYYDDD phrase when
              accessed by a COBOL program, behaves as if it had been described in a COBOL
              program as an unsigned elementary numeric integer data item seven digits in length.

          11. TIME is composed of the data elements hours, minutes, seconds, and hundredths of
              a second. TIME is based on elapsed time after midnight on a 24ΓÇôhour clock basis.
              Thus, 2:41 p.m. would be expressed as 14410000. TIME, when accessed by a
              COBOL program behaves as if it had been described in a COBOL program as an
              unsigned elementary numeric integer data item eight digits in length. The minimum
              value of TIME is 00000000; the maximum value of TIME is 23595999.

          12. DATEΓÇôTIME without the MMDDYYYY phrase is composed of the data elements
              month of year, day of month, year of century, hour of day, minute of hour, and
              second of minute. The sequence of the data element codes shall be from high order
              to low order (left to right), month of year, day of month, year in century, hour of day,
              minute of hour, and second of minute. Time is based upon elapsed time after
              midnight on a 24-hour basis. Therefore, 2:41 p.m. July 1, 1998 would be expressed
              as 070198144100. DATEΓÇôTIME without the MMDDYYYY phrase when accessed by
              a COBOL program, behaves as if it had been described in a COBOL program as an
              unsigned elementary numeric integer data item twelve digits in length.



2ΓÇô82                                                                                  7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                                     Nucleus




            DATEΓÇôTIME with the MMDDYYYY phrase is composed of the data elements month
            of year, day of month, year including century, hour of day, minute of hour, and
            second of minute. The sequence of the data element codes shall be from high order
            to low order (left to right), month of year, day of month, year including century, hour
            of day, minute of hour, and second of minute. Time is based upon elapsed time after
            midnight on a 24-hour basis. Therefore, 2:41 p.m. July 1, 1998 would be expressed
            as 07011998144100. DATEΓÇôTIME with the MMDDYYYY phrase when accessed by a
            COBOL program, behaves as if it had been described in a COBOL program as an
            unsigned elementary numeric integer data item fourteen digits in length.
           Please see 18.9 for another method for obtaining a date with a four-digit year.

2.6.5. The ADD Statement
2.6.5.1. Function
         The ADD statement causes two or more numeric operands to be summed and the result
         to be stored.

2.6.5.2. General Format
         Format 1

                    identifier-1         , identifier-2
            ADD                                               . . . TO identifier-m [ ROUNDED ]
                    literal-1            , literal-2

                   [ , identifier-n [ ROUNDED ] ] . . . [ ; ON SIZE ERROR imperative-statement ]

         Format 2

            ADD       identifier-1             identifier-2      , identifier-3
                      literal-1      ,                                            ...
                                               literal-2         , literal-3

                      GIVING identifier-m [ ROUNDED ] [ , identifier-n [ ROUNDED ] ] . . .

                      [ ; ON SIZE ERROR imperative-statement ]

         Format 3

                         CORRESPONDING
                ADD                                       identifier-1 TO identifier-2 [ ROUNDED ]
                         CORR
                [ ; ON SIZE ERROR imperative-statement ]


2.6.5.3. Syntax Rules
         1. In Formats 1 and 2, each identifier must refer to an elementary numeric item, except
            that in Format 2, each identifier following the word GIVING must refer to either an
            elementary numeric item or an elementary numericΓÇôedited item. In Format 3, each
            identifier must refer to a group item.
         2. Each literal must be a numeric literal.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                           2ΓÇô83
Nucleus




          3. The composite of operands must not contain more than 18 digits (see 2.6.3.4).
              a.   In Format 1, the composite of operands is determined by using all of the
                   operands in a given statement.
              b. In Format 2, the composite of operands is determined by using all of the
                 operands in a given statement, excluding the data items that follow the word
                 GIVING.
              c.   In Format 3, the composite of operands is determined separately for each pair of
                   corresponding data items.

          4. CORR is an abbreviation for CORRESPONDING.

2.6.5.4. General Rules
          1. See 2.6.3.1 for the ROUNDED phrase, 2.6.3.2 for the SIZE ERROR phrase, 2.6.3.3
             for the CORRESPONDING phrase, 2.6.3.4 for arithmetic statements, 2.6.3.5 for
             overlapping operands, 2.6.3.6 for multiple results in arithmetic statements, and
             2.6.3.7 for arithmetic intermediate results.
          2. If Format 1 is used, the values of the operands preceding the word TO are added
             together, then the sum is added to the current value of identifier-m storing the result
             immediately into identifier-m, and repeating this process respectively for each
             operand following the word TO.
          3. If Format 2 is used, the values of the operands preceding the word GIVING are
             added together, then the sum is stored as the new value of each identifier-m,
             identifier-n, ..., the resultantΓÇôidentifiers.
          4. If Format 3 is used, data items in identifier-1 are added to and stored in
             corresponding data items in identifier-2.
          5. The compiler insures that enough places are carried so as not to lose any significant
             digits during execution.
          6. The individual addends are decimal point aligned prior to addition. The size of such
             aligned items must not exceed 18 decimal digits.
             For example, a field defined as V9(18) cannot be added to a field defined as 9(18).
          7. As long as the aligned size of items does not exceed 18 digits, the compiler ensures
             that enough places are carried so as not to lose any significant digits during
             execution.
             For example, a field defined as S9V9(5) and 99V9(4) can be added. The intermediate
             result can be conceptually considered as S9(3)V9(5), and is therefore large enough to
             contain the result of any legal values contained in the addends.

                                                                                        Nucleus




2.6.6. The ALTER Statement
2.6.6.1. Function
         The ALTER statement modifies a predetermined sequence of operations.

2.6.6.2. General Format
           ALTER procedure-name-1 TO    [ PROCEED TO ]   procedure-name-2

                   [ , procedure-name-3   TO   [ PROCEED TO   ] procedure-name-4   ] . . .


2.6.6.3. Syntax Rules
         1. Each procedure-name-1, procedure-name-3, . . ., is the name of a paragraph that
            contains a single sentence consisting of a GO TO statement without the
            DEPENDING phrase.
         2. Each procedure-name-2, procedure-name-4, . . ., is the name of a paragraph or
            section in the Procedure Division.

2.6.6.4. General Rules
         1. Execution of the ALTER statement modifies the GO TO statement in the paragraph
            named procedure-name-1, procedure-name-3, . . ., so that subsequent executions of
            the modified GO TO statement cause transfer of control to procedure-name-2
             procedure-name-4, . . ., respectively. Modified GO TO statements in independent
            segments may, under some circumstances, be returned to their initial states (see
            9.2.2.3).
         2. A GO TO statement in a section whose segment-number is greater than or equal to
            50 must not be referred to by an ALTER statement in a section with a different
            segmentΓÇônumber.
            All other uses of the ALTER statement are valid and are performed even if
            procedure-name-1, procedure-name-3 is in an overlayable fixed segment. (See
            Section 9.)




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                2ΓÇô85
Nucleus




          For example, in the following code sequence:
          EX-HDR.
              GO TO SET-MON.
          SET-MON.
              .
              .
              .
          EX-HDR-A.
              GO TO EX-HDR-REST.
          EX-HDR-REST.
              ALTER EX-HDR-A TO PROCEED TO SET-UP-EX EX-HDR TO PROCEED TO EX-HDR-MV.

          The two GO TO paragraphs might have been switches originally set to fall through to the
          next paragraph in sequence. After being altered, EXΓÇôHDRΓÇôA will show
          GO TO SETΓÇôUPΓÇôEX, causing control to pass to the procedureΓÇôname SETΓÇôUPΓÇôEX instead
          of EXΓÇôHDRΓÇôREST. Upon completion of a specified routine, EXΓÇôHDRΓÇôA may then be
          altered back to its original status, or to some other operand by subsequent ALTER verbs.
          Note that EXΓÇôHDR and EXΓÇôHDRΓÇôA are one sentence paragraphs containing a GO TO
          statement.

          Control is transferred to the next statement in sequence, following the execution of the
          ALTER statement.

2.6.7. The COMPUTE Statement
2.6.7.1. Function

          The COMPUTE statement assigns to one or more data items the value of an arithmetic
          expression.

2.6.7.2. General Format

             COMPUTE   identifier-1   [ ROUNDED ]      [ , identifier-2 [    ROUNDED ] ]     . . .

                 = arithmetic-expression    [ ; ON SIZE ERROR     imperative-statement ]


2.6.7.3. Syntax Rules

          1. Identifiers that appear only to the left of the equal sign must refer to either an
             elementary numeric item or an elementary numeric-edited item.

2.6.7.4. General Rules

          1. See 2.6.3.1 for the ROUNDED phrase, 2.6.3.2 for the SIZE ERROR phrase, 2.6.3.4
             for arithmetic statements, 2.6.3.5 for overlapping operands, 2.6.3.6 for multiple
             results in arithmetic statements, and 2.6.3.7 for arithmetic intermediate results.
          2. An arithmetic expression consisting of a single identifier or literal provides a method
             of setting the values of identifier-1, identifier-2, etc., equal to the value of the single
             identifier or literal. (See 2.6.1.1.)


2ΓÇô86                                                                                    7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                             Nucleus




         3. If more than one identifier is specified for the result of the operation, that is,
            preceding the equal sign, the value of the arithmetic expression is computed, and
            then this value is stored as the new value of each of identifier-1, identifier-2, etc., in
            turn.
         4. The COMPUTE statement allows the user to combine arithmetic operations without
            the restrictions on composite of operands or receiving data items imposed by the
            arithmetic statements ADD, SUBTRACT, MULTIPLY, and DIVIDE.

2.6.8. The DISPLAY Statement
2.6.8.1. Function
         The DISPLAY statement causes low volume data to be transferred to an appropriate
         hardware device.

2.6.8.2. General Format

                      identifier-1     , identifier-2
         DISPLAY                                        ...   UPON mnemonic-name
                      literal-1        , literal-2

2.6.8.3. Syntax Rules
         1. The mnemonic-name is associated in the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES paragraph in the
            Environment Division to the implementor-names PRINTER, CONSOLE, and CARDΓÇô
            PUNCH.
         2. Each literal may be any figurative constant, except ALL.
         3. If the literal is numeric, then it must be an unsigned integer.

2.6.8.4. General Rules
         1. The DISPLAY statement causes the contents of each operand to be transferred to
            the hardware device in the order listed.
         2. For programs executing in batch mode, CONSOLE specifies the operatorΓÇÖs console
            and PRINTER specifies the program print file device. For programs executing in
            demand mode, CONSOLE and PRINTER both specify the demand terminal.
            CARDΓÇôPUNCH always specifies the program punch file device.
             The presence of the B option on the @XQT statement will cause a program to
             operate in batch mode for purposes of the DISPLAY statement and PADS
             (see 11.5).
         3. The maximum size of data which can be handled in a single transfer depends on the
            receiving device.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                     2ΓÇô87
Nucleus




                   Device               Size of a Single Data Transfer
                   PRINTER
                     (batch mode)                    132
                    (demand mode)                    132
                   CONSOLE
                    (batch mode)                      50
                    (demand mode)                    132
                   CARDΓÇôPUNCH                        80


          4. If a figurative constant is specified as one of the operands, only a single occurrence
             of the figurative constant is displayed.
          5. If the hardware device is capable of receiving data of the same size as the data item
             being transferred, then the data item is transferred.
          6. If the hardware device is not capable of receiving data of the same size as the data
             item being transferred, then one of the following applies:
              a.     If the size of the data item being transferred exceeds the size of the data that
                     the hardware device is capable of receiving in a single transfer, the data
                     beginning with the leftmost character is stored aligned to the left in the receiving
                     hardware device and additional data is requested. The last transfer will be
                     stored aligned to the left and space filled. In Level 1, only one transfer of data is
                     provided.
              b. If the size of the data item that the hardware device is capable of receiving
                 exceeds the size of the data being transferred, the transferred data is stored
                 aligned to the left in the receiving hardware device and space filled.
          7. When a DISPLAY statement contains more than one operand, the size of the
             sending item is the sum of the sizes associated with the operands, and the values of
             the operands are transferred in the sequence in which the operands are
             encountered.
          8. If the UPON phrase is not used, CONSOLE is assumed.
          9. Numeric items which have an assumed decimal point are converted as necessary,
             and displayed without an indication of the decimal location. Thus, a field defined as
             9(5)V9(5) will be displayed as a 10-character value.
             Binary identifiers are converted to the number of digits stated in the PICTURE clause
             before being output. Exact binary identifiers are converted to the number of decimal
             digits required by standard binary-decimal equivalence. For example, an item
             identified as 1(3) will be converted and displayed as an item identified as 9 while an
             item identified as 1(36) will be converted and displayed as an item identified as 9(10).
             Floating-point identifiers are converted to and displayed as integers with any
             fractional digits truncated. Thus, a COMPUTATIONALΓÇô1 item will be displayed as
             a 10-character number and COMPUTATIONALΓÇô2 as an 18-character number.

          Each DISPLAY statement begins a new image and continues over as many images as
          are necessary to display specified items, up to a maximum of 512 characters.

2.6.9. The DIVIDE Statement
2.6.9.1. Function
         The DIVIDE statement divides one numeric data item into others and sets the values of
         data items equal to the quotient and remainder.

2.6.9.2. General Format
         Format 1
                        identifier-1
         DIVIDE         literal-1      INTO identifier-2 [ ROUNDED ]

                 [, identifier-3 [ ROUNDED ] ] . . .    [ ; ON SIZE ERROR imperative-statement ]


         Format 2

         DIVIDE         identifier-1             identifier-2
                                        INTO                     GIVING identifier-3 [ ROUNDED ]
                        literal-1                literal-2

                 [, identifier-4 [ ROUNDED ] ] . . .     [ ; ON SIZE ERROR imperative-statement ]


         Format 3

         DIVIDE        identifier-1     BY     identifier-2     GIVING identifier-3 [ ROUNDED ]
                        literal-1              literal-2

                [, identifier-4 [ ROUNDED ] ] . . .    [ ; ON SIZE ERROR imperative-statement ]

         Format 4

                        identifier-1             identifier-2
           DIVIDE                       INTO                     GIVING identifier-3 [ ROUNDED ]
                        literal-1                literal-2

                 REMAINDER identifier-4 [ ; ON SIZE ERROR imperative-statement ]




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                          2ΓÇô89
Nucleus




          Format 5


            DIVIDE    identifier-1           identifier-2
                                     BY                     GIVING identifier-3 [ ROUNDED ]
                       literal-1             literal-2

                REMAINDER identifier-4 [ ; ON SIZE ERROR imperative-statement ]


2.6.9.3. Syntax Rules
          1. Each identifier must refer to an elementary numeric item, except that any identifier
             associated with the GIVING or REMAINDER phrase must refer to either an
             elementary numeric item or an elementary numeric-edited item.
          2. Each literal must be a numeric literal.
          3. The composite of operands, which is the hypothetical data item resulting from the
             superimposition of all receiving data items (except the REMAINDER data item) of a
             given statement aligned on their decimal points, must not contain more than
             eighteen digits.

2.6.9.4. General Rules
          1. See 2.6.3.1 for the ROUNDED phrase, 2.6.3.2 for the SIZE ERROR phrase, 2.6.3.4
             for arithmetic statements, 2.6.3.5 for overlapping operands, 2.6.3.6 for multiple
             results in arithmetic statements, and 2.6.3.7 for arithmetic intermediate results.
             See also general rules 5 through 7 which follow for a discussion of the ROUNDED
             phrase and the SIZE ERROR phrase as they pertain to Formats 4 and 5.
          2. When Format 1 is used, the value of identifier-1 or literal-1 is divided into the value of
             identifier-2. The value of the dividend (identifier-2) is replaced by this quotient; this is
             done similarly for identifier-1 or literal-1 and identifier-3, etc.
          3. When Format 2 is used, the value of identifier-1 or literal-1 is divided into identifier-2
             or literal-2 and the result is stored in identifier-3, identifier-4, etc.
          4. When Format 3 is used, the value of identifier-1 or literal-1 is divided by the value of
             identifier-2 or literal-2 and the result is stored in identifier-3, identifier-4, etc.
          5. Formats 4 and 5 are used when a remainder from the division operation is desired,
             namely identifier-4. The remainder in ASCII COBOL is defined as the result of
             subtracting the product of the quotient (identifier-3) and the divisor from the
             dividend. If identifier-3 is defined as a numeric-edited item, the quotient used to
             calculate the remainder is an intermediate field which contains the unedited
             quotient. If ROUNDED is used, the quotient used to calculate the remainder is an
             intermediate field which contains the quotient of the DIVIDE statement, truncated
             rather than rounded.
          6. In Formats 4 and 5, the accuracy of the REMAINDER data item (identifier-4) is
             defined by the calculation described above. Appropriate decimal alignment and
             truncation (not rounding) will be performed for the content of the data item
             referenced by identifier-4, as needed.




2ΓÇô90                                                                                    7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                            Nucleus




         7. When the ON SIZE ERROR phrase is used in Formats 4 and 5, the following rules
            pertain:

             a.    If the size error occurs on the quotient, no remainder calculation is meaningful.
                   Thus, the contents of the data items referenced by both identifier-3 and
                   identifier-4 will remain unchanged.
             b. If the size error occurs on the remainder, the contents of the data item
                referenced by identifier-4 remains unchanged. However, as with other instances
                of multiple results of arithmetic statements, the user will have to do his own
                analysis to recognize which situation has actually occurred.

         In the example:
            DIVIDE A BY B GIVING C REMAINDER D

         if the fields are defined as:
            A: 99V9

            B: 9V99

            C: 9999V99

            D: 9V99

         and contain only legal numeric values, no truncation or size error condition should arise,
         except for the zero divisor case.

2.6.10. The EXIT Statement
2.6.10.1. Function
         The EXIT statement provides a common end point for a series of procedures.

2.6.10.2. General Format
           EXIT.


2.6.10.3. Syntax Rules
         1. The EXIT statement must appear in a sentence by itself.
         2. The EXIT sentence must be the only sentence in the paragraph.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                    2ΓÇô91
Nucleus




2.6.10.4. General Rules
          1. An EXIT statement assigns a procedure-name to a given point in a program. An EXIT
             statement has no other effect on the compilation or execution of the program.
          The following example shows the case of the simple EXIT as a common transfer point.

                  .
                  .
                  .
                 MOVE 1 TO A.
                 MOVE 9 TO B.
                 PERFORM PARA1 THRU PARA2.
                 .
                 .
                 .
            PARA1.
                IF A = 0 GO TO PARA2.
                ADD 1 TO A.
                IF A = B GO TO PARA2.
                GO TO PARA1.
            PARA2.
                EXIT.
            PARA3.


2.6.11. The GO TO Statement
2.6.11.1. Function
          The GO TO statement causes control to be transferred from one part of the Procedure
          Division to another.

2.6.11.2. General Format
          Format 1
            GO TO [    procedure-name-1   ]

          Format 2
            GO TO procedure-name-1 [ ,    procedure-name-2 ] . . . , procedure-name-n

                     DEPENDING ON identifier


2.6.11.3. Syntax Rules
          1. Identifier is the name of a numeric elementary item described without any positions
             to the right of the assumed decimal point.
          2. When a paragraph is referenced by an ALTER statement, that paragraph can consist
             only of a paragraph header followed by a Format 1 GO TO statement.




2ΓÇô92                                                                               7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                               Nucleus




         3. A Format 1 GO TO statement, without procedure-name-1, can only appear in a single
            statement paragraph.
         4. If a GO TO statement represented by Format 1 appears in a consecutive sequence
            of imperative statements within a sentence, it must appear as the last statement in
            that sequence.

2.6.11.4. General Rules
         1. When a GO TO statement, represented by Format 1 is executed, control is
            transferred to procedure-name-1 or to another procedureΓÇôname if the GO TO
            statement has been modified by an ALTER statement.
         2. If procedure-name-1 is not specified in Format 1, an ALTER statement, referring to
            this GO TO statement, must be executed prior to the execution of this GO TO
            statement.
         3. When a GO TO statement represented by Format 2 is executed, control is
            transferred to procedure-name-1, procedure-name-2, etc., depending on the value of
            the identifier being 1, 2, . . . n. If the value of the identifier is anything other than the
            positive or unsigned integers 1, 2, . . . n, then no transfer occurs and control passes
            to the next statement in the normal sequence for execution.

2.6.12. The IF Statement
2.6.12.1. Function
         The IF statement causes a condition (see 2.6.1.2) to be evaluated. The subsequent
         action of the object program depends on whether the value of the condition is true or
         false.

2.6.12.2. General Format
         IF condition ;   statement-1               ; ELSE statement-2
                          NEXT SENTENCE             ; ELSE NEXT SENTENCE

2.6.12.3. Syntax Rules
         1. Statement-1 and statement-2 represent either an imperative statement or a
            conditional statement, and either may be followed by a conditional statement.
         2. The ELSE NEXT SENTENCE phrase may be omitted if it immediately precedes the
            terminal period of the sentence.

2.6.12.4. General Rules
         1. When an IF statement is executed, the following transfers of control occur:
             a.   If the condition is true, statement-1 is executed if specified. If statement-1
                  contains a procedure branching or conditional statement, control is explicitly
                  transferred in accordance with the rules of that statement. (See 1.3.8.2.4.) If
                  statement-1 does not contain a procedure branching or conditional statement,
                  the ELSE phrase, if specified, is ignored and control passes to the next
                  executable sentence.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                       2ΓÇô93
Nucleus




              b. If the condition is true and the NEXT SENTENCE phrase is specified instead of
                 statement-1, the ELSE phrase, if specified, is ignored and control passes to the
                 next executable sentence.
              c.   If the condition is false, statement-1 or its surrogate NEXT SENTENCE is
                   ignored, and statement-2, if specified, is executed. If statement-2 contains a
                   procedure branching or conditional statement, control is explicitly transferred in
                   accordance with the rules of that statement. (See 1.3.8.2.4.) If statement-2
                   does not contain a procedure branching or conditional statement, control passes
                   to the next executable sentence. If the ELSE statement-2 phrase is not
                   specified, statement-1 is ignored and control passes to the next executable
                   sentence.
              d. If the condition is false, and the ELSE NEXT SENTENCE phrase is specified,
                 statement-1 is ignored, if specified, and control passes to the next executable
                 sentence.
          2. Statement-1 and/or statement-2 may contain an IF statement. In this case the IF
             statement is said to be nested.

          IF statements within IF statements may be considered as paired IF and ELSE
          combinations, proceeding from left to right. Thus, any ELSE encountered is considered
          to apply to the immediately preceding IF that has not been already paired with an ELSE.

          For example:

            IF condition-1 statement-1
                IF condition-2
                     IF condition-3 statement-2
                     ELSE statement-3
                 ELSE statement-4
                     IF condition-4
                          IF condition-5 statement-5
                          ELSE statement-6
                               IF condition-6 NEXT SENTENCE
                               ELSE statement-7.
            New sentence.


          The correspondence of IFs and ELSEs is shown by indentation, a frequently used means
          of making such complex sentences more readable.

          The execution of this example, shown in the flowchart in Figure 2-12, assumes that no
          statement contains a GO TO.

         The INSPECT statement provides the ability to tally (Format 1), replace (Format 2), or
         tally and replace (Format 3) occurrences of single characters or groups of characters in a
         data item.

2.6.13.2. General Format
         Format 1
    INSPECT identifier-1        TALLYING

                                          ALL      identifier-3                               identifier-4
       , identifier-2 FOR            ,    LEADING   literal-1             BEFORE INITIAL                          ...
                                                                                              literal-2                 ...
                                                                          AFTER
                                          CHARACTERS

Nucleus




               Format 2
       INSPECT identifier-1            REPLACING


          CHARACTERS BY                  identifier-6             BEFORE        INITIAL      identifier-7
                                         literal-4                AFTER                      literal-5

                   ALL
                   LEADING             identifier-5          identifier-6     BEFORE                   identifier-7
           ,                   ,                        BY                                INITIAL                        ...    ...
                   FIRST                literal-3              literal-4      AFTER                    literal-5


               Format 3

       INSPECT identifier-1        TALLYING

                                              ALL      identifier-3
               , identifier-2 FOR                      literal-1                BEFORE       INITIAL      identifier-4
                                          ,   LEADING                                                                     ...    ...
                                                                                AFTER                     literal-2
                                              CHARACTERS

                   REPLACING

               CHARACTERS BY                  identifier-6             BEFORE                       identifier-7
                                                                                  INITIAL
                                              literal-4                AFTER                        literal-5
                    ALL
               ,    LEADING             identifier-5    BY     identifier-6     BEFORE       INITIAL identifier-7
                                   ,
                    FIRST                literal-3             literal-4        AFTER                literal-5           ...    ...


2.6.13.3. Syntax Rules

               All Formats:
               1. Identifier-1 must reference either a group item or any category of elementary item,
                  described (either implicitly or explicitly) as usage is DISPLAY.
               2. Identifier-3 . . . identifier-n must reference either an elementary alphabetic,
                  alphanumeric or numeric item described (either implicitly or explicitly) as usage is
                  DISPLAY.
               3. Each literal must be nonnumeric and may be any figurative constant, except ALL.
               4. In Level 1, literal-1, literal-2, literal-3, literal-4, and literal-5, and the data items
                  referenced by identifier-3, identifier-4, identifier-5, identifier-6, and identifier-7 must
                  be one character in length.
                     Except as specifically noted in syntax and general rules, this restriction on length
                     does not apply to Level 2.

               Formats 1 and 3 only:
               5. Identifier-2 must reference an elementary numeric data item.
               6. If either literal-1 or literal-2 is a figurative constant, the figurative constant refers to an
                  implicit one character data item.
