15.4. Procedure Division
15.4.1. The CLOSE Statement
15.4.1.1. Function
        The CLOSE statement terminates the processing of reels/units and files with optional
        rewind and/or lock where applicable.

15.4.1.2. General Format
                                      REEL
                                      UNIT            WITH NO REWIND
        CLOSE file-name-1
                                                      NO REWIND
                                      WITH
                                                      LOCK


                                      REEL
                                                      WITH NO REWIND
                                      UNIT                                          ...
                 , file-name-2
                                                      NO REWIND
                                      WITH
                                                      LOCK

15.4.1.3. Syntax Rule
        The files referenced in the CLOSE statement need not all have the same organization or
        access.

15.4.1.4. General Rules
        Except where otherwise stated in the general rules that follow, the terms ΓÇ£reelΓÇ¥ and
        ΓÇ£unitΓÇ¥ are synonymous and completely interchangeable in the CLOSE statement.
        1. A CLOSE statement may only be executed for a file in an open mode.
        2. For the purpose of showing the effect of various types of CLOSE statements as
           applied to various storage media, all files are divided into the following categories:
            a.    Sequential single-reel/unit. A sequential file that is entirely contained on one
                  reel/unit.
            b. Sequential multi-reel/unit. A sequential file that is contained on more than one
               reel/unit.
        3. The results of executing each type of CLOSE for each category of file are
           summarized in Table 15-4.




15ΓÇô20                                                                                 7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                             IBM Tape Processing




                Table 15-4. Relationship of Categories of Files and the Formats
                                    of the CLOSE Statement


                                                                     File Category

                    CLOSE Statement Format                  Sequential         Sequential
                                                         Single-Reel/Unit     Multi-Reel/Unit

                CLOSE                                           F                    C,F,A
                CLOSE WITH LOCK                                F,D                   C,F,E,A
                CLOSE WITH NO REWIND                           C,B                   C,B,A
                CLOSE REEL/UNIT                                 X                     E,F
                CLOSE REEL/UNIT WITH NO REWIND                  X                      E



            The definitions of the symbols in the table follow. Where the definition depends on
            whether the file is an input or output file, alternate definitions are given; otherwise, a
            definition applies to input and output files.

            A. Previous Reels/Units Unaffected

                 Input Files:

                 All reels/units in the file prior to the current reel/unit are processed according to
                 the standard reel/unit swap procedure, except those reels/units controlled by a
                 prior CLOSE REEL/UNIT statement. If the current reel/unit is not the last in the
                 file, the reels/units in the file following the current one are not processed. (See
                 Appendix E.)

                 Output Files:

                 All reels/units in the file prior to the current reel/unit are processed according to
                 the standard reel/unit swap procedure, except those reels/units controlled by a
                 prior CLOSE REEL/UNIT statement. (See Appendix E.)

            B. No Rewind of Current Reel

                  The current reel/unit is left in its current position.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                    15ΓÇô21
IBM Tape Processing




           C. Close File

              Input Files:

              If the file is positioned at its end and label records are specified for the file, the
              labels are processed according to the standard label convention. The behavior of
              the CLOSE statement when label records are specified but not present, or when
              label records are not specified but are present, is undefined. Closing operations
              are executed. If the file is positioned at its end and label records are not
              specified for the file, label processing does not take place but other closing
              operations are executed. If the file is positioned other than at its end, the
              closing operations are executed, but there is no ending label processing. (See
              Appendix E.)

              Output Files:

              If label records are specified for the file, the labels are processed according to
              the standard label convention. The behavior of the CLOSE statement when label
              records are specified but not present, or when label records are not specified but
              are present, is undefined. Closing operations are executed. If label records are
              not specified for the file, label processing does not take place but other closing
              operations are executed. (See Appendix E.)

           D. File Lock

              This file cannot be opened again during this execution of this run unit.

           E. Close Reel/Unit

              Input Files:

              The following operations take place:

              1. A reel/unit swap.

              2. The standard beginning reel/unit label procedure is executed.

              The next executed READ statement for that file makes available the next data
              record on the new reel/unit.

              Output Files:

              The following operations take place:

              1. The standard ending reel/unit label procedure is executed.

              2. A reel/unit swap.

              3. The standard beginning reel/unit label procedure is executed.

                  The next executed WRITE statement that references that file directs the
                  next logical data record to the next reel/unit of the file.


15ΓÇô22                                                                              7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                             IBM Tape Processing




             F   Rewind

                 The current reel is positioned at its physical beginning.

             X   Illegal

                 This is an illegal combination of a CLOSE option and a file category.
                 The results at object time are undefined.

         4. The action taken if the file is in the open mode when a STOP RUN statement is
            executed or the action taken for a file that has been opened in a called program and
            not closed in that program prior to the execution of a CANCEL statement for that
            program are undefined. No implicit CLOSE procedures will be initiated. This could
            result in the condition which would cause the file to be unusable on subsequent
            accesses to it.
         5. If the OPTIONAL phrase has been specified for the file in the FILEΓÇô CONTROL
            paragraph of the Environment Division and the file is not present, the standard endΓÇô
            ofΓÇôfile processing is not performed for that file.
         6. If a CLOSE statement without the REEL or UNIT phrase has been executed for a file,
            no other statement (except the SORT or MERGE statements with the USING or
            GIVING phrases) can be executed that references that file, either explicitly or
            implicitly, unless an intervening OPEN statement for that file is executed.
         7. Following the successful execution of a CLOSE statement without the REEL or UNIT
            phrase, the record area associated with fileΓÇôname is no longer available. The
            unsuccessful execution of such a CLOSE statement leaves the availability of the
            record area undefined.

15.4.2. The OPEN Statement
15.4.2.1. Function
         The OPEN statement initiates the processing of files. It also performs checking and
         writing of labels and other input-output operations.

15.4.2.2. General Format
           INPUT file-name-1 [ WITH NO REWIND ] [ , file-name-2 [ WITH NO REWIND ] ] . . .
  OPEN                                                                                         ...
           OUTPUT file-name-3 [ WITH NO REWIND ] [ , file-name-4 [ WITH NO REWIND ] ] . . .


15.4.2.3. Syntax Rule
         The files referenced in the OPEN statement need not all have the same organization or
         access.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                15ΓÇô23
IBM Tape Processing




15.4.2.4. General Rules
        1. The successful execution of an OPEN statement determines the availability of the
           file and results in the file being in an open mode.
        2. The successful execution of an OPEN statement makes the associated record area
           available to the program.
        3. Prior to the successful execution of an OPEN statement for a given file, no
           statement (except for a SORT or MERGE statement with the USING or GIVING
           phrases) can be executed that references that file, either explicitly or implicitly.
        4. An OPEN statement must be successfully executed prior to the execution of any of
           the permissible input-output statements. In Table 15-5, an ΓÇ£XΓÇ¥ at an intersection
           indicates that the specified statement, used in the sequential access mode, may be
           used with the sequential file organization and open mode given at the top of the
           column.


                     Table 15-5. Permissible Statements

                                               Open Mode
                    Statement            Input           Output
                    READ                   X
                    WRITE                                   X



        5. A file may be opened with the INPUT and OUTPUT phrases in the same program.
           Following the initial execution of an OPEN statement for a file, each subsequent
           OPEN statement execution for that same file must be preceded by the execution of
           a CLOSE statement, without the REEL, UNIT, or LOCK phrase, for that file.
        6. Execution of the OPEN statement does not obtain or release the first data record.
        7. If label records are specified for the file (see Appendix E), the beginning labels are
           processed as follows:
            a.   When the INPUT phrase is specified, the execution of the OPEN statement
                 causes the labels to be checked in accordance with the conventions for input
                 label checking.
            b. When the OUTPUT phrase is specified, the execution of the OPEN statement
               causes the labels to be written in accordance with the conventions for output
               label writing.
            The behavior of the OPEN statement when label records are specified but not
            present, or when label records are not specified but are present, is undefined.
        8. The file description entry for file-name-1 or file-name-2 must be equivalent to that
           used when this file was created.
        9. If an input file is designated with the OPTIONAL phrase in its SELECT clause, the
           object program causes an interrogation for the presence or absence of this file. If
           the file is not present, the first READ statement for this file causes the AT END
           condition to occur. (See 15.4.3.)


15ΓÇô24                                                                               7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                             IBM Tape Processing




         10. The NO REWIND phrase can only be used with sequential single reel/unit files. (See
             15.4.1.)
         11. Since the storage medium for the file permits rewinding, the following rules apply:
             a.   When the NO REWIND phrase is not specified, execution of the OPEN
                  statement causes the file to be positioned at its beginning.
             b. When the NO REWIND phrase is specified, execution of the OPEN statement
                does not cause the file to be repositioned; the file must be already positioned at
                its beginning prior to execution of the OPEN statement.
         12. For files being opened with the INPUT phrase, the OPEN statement sets the current
             record pointer to the first record currently existing within the file. If no record exists
             in the file, the current record pointer is set such that the next executed READ
             statement for the file will result in an AT END condition.
         13. Upon successful execution of an OPEN statement with the OUTPUT phrase
             specified, a file is created. At that time the associated file contains no data records.

15.4.3. The READ Statement
15.4.3.1. Function
         The READ statement makes available the next logical record from a file.

15.4.3.2. General Format
           READ file-name RECORD [ INTO identifier ] ; AT END imperative-statement


15.4.3.3. Syntax Rule
         The INTO phrase must not be used when the input file contains logical records of various
         sizes as indicated by their record descriptions. The storage area associated with
         identifier and the record area associated with fileΓÇôname must not be the same storage
         area.

15.4.3.4. General Rules
         1. The associated file must be open in the INPUT mode at the time this statement is
            executed. (See 15.4.2.)
         2. The record to be made available by the READ statement is determined as follows:
             a.   If the current record pointer was positioned by the execution of the OPEN
                  statement, the record pointed to by the current record pointer is made available.
             b. If the current record pointer was positioned by the execution of a previous READ
                statement, the current record pointer is updated to point to the next existing
                record in the file and then that record is made available.
         3. Regardless of the method used to overlap access time with processing time, the
            concept of the READ statement is unchanged in that a record is available to the
            object program prior to the execution of any statement following the READ
            statement.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                    15ΓÇô25
IBM Tape Processing




        4. When the logical records of a file are described with more than one record
           description, these records share the same storage area. This is equivalent to an
           implicit redefinition of the area. The contents of any data items which lie beyond the
           range of the current data record are undefined at the completion of the execution of
           the READ statement.
        5. If the INTO phrase is specified, the record being read is moved from the record area
           to the area specified by identifier according to the rules specified for the MOVE
           statement without the CORRESPONDING phrase. The implied MOVE does not
           occur if the execution of the READ statement was unsuccessful. Any subscripting
           or indexing associated with identifier is evaluated after the record has been read and
           immediately before it is moved to the data item.
        6. When the INTO phrase is used, the record being read is available in both the input
           record area and the data area associated with identifier.
        7. If, at the time of execution of a READ statement, the position of current record
           pointer for that file is undefined, the execution of that READ statement is
           unsuccessful.
        8. If the end of a reel or unit is recognized during execution of a READ statement, and
           the logical end of the file has not been reached, the following operations are
           executed:
            a.   The standard ending reel/unit label procedure. (See Appendix E.)
            b. A reel/unit swap.
            c.   The standard beginning reel/unit label procedure. (See Appendix E.)
            d. The first data record of the new reel/unit is made available.
        9. If a file described with the OPTIONAL phrase is not present at the time the file is
           opened, then at the time of execution of the first READ statement for the file, the AT
           END condition occurs and the execution of the READ statement is unsuccessful.
           The standard end-of-file procedures are not performed. (See 15.2.1.1 and 15.4.2.)
           Execution of the program then proceeds as specified in general rule 11.
        10. If, at the time of the execution of a READ statement, no next logical record exists in
            the file, the AT END condition occurs, and the execution of the READ statement is
            considered unsuccessful.
        11. When the AT END condition is recognized, control is transferred to the AT END
            imperative-statement.
            When the AT END condition occurs, execution of the inputΓÇôoutput statement which
            caused the condition is unsuccessful.
        12. Following the unsuccessful execution of any READ statement, the contents of the
            associated record area and the position of the current record pointer are undefined.
        13. When the AT END condition has been recognized, a READ statement for that file
            must not be executed without first executing a successful CLOSE statement
            followed by the execution of a successful OPEN statement for that file.




15ΓÇô26                                                                               7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                          IBM Tape Processing




15.4.4. The WRITE Statement
15.4.4.1. Function
         The WRITE statement releases a logical record for an output file.

15.4.4.2. General Format
           WRITE record-name [ FROM identifier ]


15.4.4.3. Syntax Rules
         1. Record-name and identifier must not reference the same storage area.
         2. The record-name is the name of a logical record in the File Section of the Data
            Division and may be qualified.

15.4.4.4. General Rules
         1. The associated file must be open in the OUTPUT mode at the time of the execution
            of this statement. (See 15.4.2.)
         2. The logical record released by the execution of the WRITE statement is no longer
            available in the record area unless the associated file is named in a SAME RECORD
            AREA clause or the execution of the WRITE statement was unsuccessful due to a
            boundary violation. The logical record is also available to the program as a record of
            other files referenced in the same SAME RECORD AREA clause as the associated
            output file, as well as to the file associated with record-name.
         3. The results of the execution of the WRITE statement with the FROM phrase is
            equivalent to the execution of:
             a.   The statement:
                    MOVE identifier TO record-name

                  according to the rules specified for the MOVE statement, followed by:
             b. The same WRITE statement without the FROM phrase.
             The contents of the record area prior to the execution of the implicit MOVE
             statement have no effect on the execution of this WRITE statement.
             After execution of the WRITE statement is complete, the information in the area
             referenced by identifier is available, even though the information in the area
             referenced by record-name may not be. (See general rule 2.)
         4. The current record pointer is unaffected by the execution of a WRITE statement.
         5. The maximum record size for a file is established at the time the file is created and
            must not subsequently be changed.
         6. The execution of the WRITE statement releases a logical record to the operating
            system.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                 15ΓÇô27
IBM Tape Processing




        7. After the recognition of an end-of-reel or an end-of-unit of an output file that is
           contained on more than one physical reel/unit, the WRITE statement performs the
           following operations:
            a.   The standard ending reel/unit label procedure. (See Appendix E.)
            b. A reel/unit swap.
            c.   The standard beginning reel/unit label procedure. (See Appendix E.)




15ΓÇô28                                                                               7830 7709ΓÇô002

15.5. IBM Tape File Assignment
         The link between the ASCII COBOL defined file name and the OS 2200 File Control
         System name should be specified in the runstream (@ASG or @USE) prior to the
         execution of any program containing IBM tape file processing.

15.5.1. Assignment Rules
         1. The file must be assigned to a valid tape device.
         2. The Q (quarter-word) data transfer format must be specified in the files assignment.
         3. When hardware translation is specified, the processor code must be ASCII and the
            tape code must be EBCDIC.
         4. The presence of the J option in the fileΓÇÖs assignment will cause ASCII COBOL to
            process the fileΓÇÖs labels. (See E.3.2). For ASCII COBOL to process the labels, Exec
            configuration tag TLEBCDIC must be set to 0 or 1. TLEBCDIC set to 1 is preferred.
         5. The absence of the J option in the fileΓÇÖs assignment will cause the Exec (40R3 and
            higher) to process the fileΓÇÖs labels. (See E.3.2). For the Exec to process the labels,
            Exec configuration tag TLEBCDIC must be set to 1 or 2. TLEBCDIC set to 1 is
            preferred.

         For more information, see the Exec System Software Installation and Configuration
         Guide.

15.5.2. Assignment Examples
         The following are specific examples of the OS 2200 Executive @ASG control statements
         for IBM tape files. Consult the OS 2200 Executive System Software Executive Control
         Language (ECL) End Use and Programming Reference Manual (7830 7949) for general
         rules and formats.

           @ASG,TJ IBM1.,U9S//////Q,5678

           @ASG,T IBM2.,U9S//////Q,2345

           @ASG,TJ IBM3.,U9V////ASCII/EBCDIC/Q,SCRTCH

           @ASG,T IBM4.,HICL//////Q////BUFON,483




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                 15ΓÇô29
IBM Tape Processing




15.5.3. COBOL Program Links
        The links between the COBOL-defined files and the File Control System files named in
        15.5.2 are provided by the following COBOL source language statements:
          SELECT IBM-FILE ASSIGN TO UNISERVO IBM1.

          SELECT EBCDIC ASSIGN TO UNISERVO IBM2.

          SELECT IBM-HT ASSIGN TO UNISERVO IBM3.

          SELECT IBM-CART ASSIGN TO UNISERVO IBM4.

        The COBOL file IBMΓÇôFILE would be linked with an unlabeled tape number 5678 with the
        File Control System name IBM1.

        The COBOL file EBCDIC would now be associated with labeled tape number 2345 with
        the File Control System name IBM2.

        The COBOL file IBMΓÇôHT would now be associated with an unlabeled SCRTCH tape with
        the File Control System name IBM3, and will be hardwareΓÇôtranslated to and from ASCII
        and EBCDIC.

        The COBOL file IBMΓÇôCART would now be linked with labeled tape 483, where tape 483
        is a half-inch cartridge volume assigned to a 0899 cartridge tape device in buffered write
        mode.

15.6. EBCDIC Character Codes
         The EBCDIC character codes for the characters ΓÇÿ!ΓÇÖ, ΓÇÿ[ΓÇÖ and ΓÇÿ]ΓÇÖ differ depending upon the
         operating system (OS/3 vs. IBM OS/360). When processing EBCDIC data, the ASCII
         COBOL run-time library defaults to the OS/3 character code set. If an IBM OS/360
         character code set is needed, an ASCII COBOL build must be performed to apply a local
         change to the run-time library element C$DJAE (change tag OS3$ to zero).

         If hardware translation is specified, the OS/3 character code set is always used.

Section 16
Information Interchange Tape
Processing Module


16.1. General
         The Information Interchange Tape Processing Module is a subset of the Sequential IΓÇôO
         Module which refers to tape files. Except for the restrictions imposed by this section, all
         formats, syntax rules and general rules which apply to tape files also apply to Information
         Interchange files. However, the formats, syntax rules, and general rules that apply to
         Information Interchange files are Unisys defined.

         The Information Interchange Tape Processing Module is specifically designed to process
         tapes which are in the formats described in the X3.27ΓÇô1987 (R 1998) Magnetic Tape
         Labels for Information Interchange. Tapes in this format are preferred for exchange of
         data between the systems of different computer manufacturers.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                  16ΓÇô1
Information Interchange Tape Processing Module




16.2. Environment Division
16.2.1. InputΓÇôOutput Section
16.2.2. The FILEΓÇôCONTROL Paragraph
16.2.2.1. Function
        The FILEΓÇôCONTROL paragraph names each file and allows specification of other
        file-related information.

16.2.2.2. General Format
          FILE-CONTROL. { file-control-entry }     . . .


16.2.3. The File Control Entry
16.2.3.1. Function
        The file control entry names a file and may specify other file-related information.

16.2.3.2. General Format
        SELECT [ OPTIONAL ] file-name

             ASSIGN TO implementor-name-1 [ , implementor-name-2 ] . . .

               ; RESERVE integer-1      AREA
                                        AREAS

             [ ; ORGANIZATION IS SEQUENTIAL ]

             [ ; ACCESS MODE IS SEQUENTIAL ]

             [ ; FILE STATUS IS data-name-1 ] .

16.2.3.3. Syntax Rules
        1. The SELECT clause must be specified first in the file control entry. The clauses that
           follow the SELECT clause may appear in any order.
        2. Each file described in the Data Division must be named once and only once as file-
           name in the FILEΓÇôCONTROL paragraph. Each file specified in the file control entry
           must have a file description entry in the Data Division.
        3. The only allowable implementor-name-1 is INTERCHANGE.
        4. If implementor-name-2 is specified, it is a 1- to 12-character name used to link the
           COBOL file to OS 2200 Executive File Control and should appear on an @ASG or
           @USE statement in the run stream for executing the object program.
        5. When implementor-name-2 is not specified, the first 12 characters of file-name are
           used to link the COBOL file to OS 2200 Executive File Control.
        6. All recursions of implementor-name-1, implementor-name-2, are for documentation
           only.

         7. If the ACCESS MODE clause is not specified, the ACCESS MODE IS SEQUENTIAL
            clause is implied.
         8. Data-name-1 must be defined in the Data Division as a 2-character data item of the
            category alphanumeric and must not be defined in the File Section, the Report
            Section, or the Communication Section. Data-name-1 must be defined as USAGE
            DISPLAY.
         9. Data-name-1 may be qualified.
         10. When the ORGANIZATION IS SEQUENTIAL clause is not specified, the
             ORGANIZATION IS SEQUENTIAL clause is implied.
         11. The OPTIONAL phrase may only be specified for input files. Its specification is
             required for input files that are not necessarily present each time the object program
             is executed.

16.2.3.4. General Rules
         1. The ASSIGN clause specifies the association of the file referenced by file-name to a
            storage medium.
         2. If the RESERVE clause is specified, it is for documentation only. Two input-output
            areas are always allocated.
         3. The ORGANIZATION clause specifies the logical structure of a file. The file
            organization is established at the time a file is created and cannot subsequently be
            changed.
         4. Records in the file are accessed in the sequence dictated by the file organization.
            This sequence is specified by predecessor-successor record relationship established
            by the execution of WRITE statements when the file is created or extended.
         5. When the FILE STATUS clause is specified, a value will be moved by the ASCII
            COBOL runtime system into the data item specified by data-name-1 after the
            execution of every statement that references that file either explicitly or implicitly.
            This value indicates the status of execution of the statement. (See 4.1.3.4.)

Information Interchange Tape Processing Module




16.3. Data Division
16.3.1. File Section
16.3.2. The RECORDING MODE Clause
16.3.2.1. Function
        The RECORDING MODE clause is used to specify a tape format specified in X3.27ΓÇô1987
        (R1998) Magnetic Tape Labels for Information Interchange.

16.3.2.2. General Format
                                  D
                                  F
        RECORDING MODE IS         S
                                  U

16.3.2.3. General Rule
        The structure of the physical data blocks may be defined by one of the following:
        1. The D phrase specifies variable length blocked records.
        2. The F phrase specifies fixed blocked records.
        3. The S phrase specifies spanned blocked records.
        4. The U phrase specifies variable length unblocked records.

16.3.3. Record Description Restrictions
        Data items in a record description for an INTERCHANGE file abide by the following
        restrictions:
        ΓÇó   The usage for each data item must be DISPLAY.
        ΓÇó   The description of each signed numeric data item must include the SIGN IS
            LEADING SEPARATE CHARACTER clause.




16ΓÇô4                                                                             7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                      Information Interchange Tape Processing Module




16.4. Information Interchange Tape File Assignment
         The link between the ASCII COBOL defined file name and the OS 2200 File Control
         System name should be specified in the runstream (@ASG or @USE) prior to the
         execution of any program containing Information Interchange tape file processing.

16.4.1. Assignment Examples
         The following are specific examples of the OS 2200 Executive @ASG control statements
         for Information Interchange files. Consult OS 2200 Exec System Software Executive
         Requests Programming Reference Manual (7830 7899) for general rules and formats.
           @ASG,T TAPE3.,HICL//////Q,1234

           @ASG,TJ TAPE4.,HIS//////Q,9012


16.4.2. COBOL Program Links
         The links between COBOL-defined files and the File Control System files named in
         16.4.1 are provided in the following COBOL source language statements:
           SELECT NAME-FILE ASSIGN TO INTERCHANGE TAPE3.

           SELECT INTERCHANGE-FILE ASSIGN TO INTERCHANGE TAPE4.

         The COBOL file NAMEΓÇôFILE would be associated with labeled tape number 1234 which
         has the File Control System name TAPE3.

         The COBOL file INTERCHANGEΓÇôFILE would be associated with unlabeled tape number
         9012 which has the File Control System name TAPE4.

Section 17
Optimization


17.1. General
         COBOL programmers can easily optimize a COBOL program by utilizing the language
         features and hints documented in this section.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                          17ΓÇô1
Optimization




17.2. Programming Hints
        This section contains a collection of hints for writing efficient and maintainable COBOL
        programs. Many of these suggestions may be found in the other sections of this
        document and many are common sense approaches to good COBOL programming
        techniques. The majority of the following recommendations are based on the COBOL
        language and should, therefore, apply to most COBOL compilers. Others, however, are
        based on special considerations for the OS 2200 Executive environment or for the ASCII
        COBOL implementation.

17.2.1. Program Maintainability
        1. Do not use the ALTER statement.
        2. Use meaningful names. Do not use numeric paragraph and section names.
        3. Avoid the use of the OPEN REVERSED facility.
        4. Use 01 level-number instead of the 77 level-number.
        5. Use the Report Writer facility for report generation.
        6. Use the COPY statement for common data structures and common procedures.
        7. Use comment lines freely.
        8. Use indentation to clearly depict the control flow of conditional statements.
        9. The readability (and maintainability) of a program will be improved if structured
           control statements (for example, IF, PERFORM) are used in place of GO TO
           statements in as many instances as possible.

17.2.2. Execution Speed
        Increased execution speed can generally be obtained in the following areas.

17.2.2.1. General
        1. Moves and arithmetic operations are performed faster on unsigned data than signed
           data.
        2. Arithmetic operations are generally faster if they are done on binary fields
           (COMPUTATIONAL). If input is in characters, yet considerable calculations are done,
           it is more efficient to force a conversion by moving DISPLAY data items to
           appropriate COMPUTATIONAL items, and then reference the COMPUTATIONAL
           items in arithmetic statements or expressions.
        3. Where possible, grouping of references to the same operands enables the compiler
           to better optimize generated code.
        4. The use of multiple receiving fields is more efficient than repeating calculations.




17ΓÇô2                                                                               7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                     Optimization




         5. When multiple receiving fields are stated they should be grouped by usage and size,
            and the groups arranged in an order to simplify conversion. That is, if a COMPUTE
            will result in a single precision floating-point intermediate result, receiving fields
            should be ordered.
             a.   Floating-point
             b. Binary, grouping like size items together
             c.   DISPLAY or COMPUTATIONALΓÇô3
             If the computation produces a DISPLAY result, the order of receiving fields should be
             reversed.
         6. Indexing is more efficient than subscripting.
         7. Group and alphanumeric moves are faster than numeric moves.
         8. PERFORM VARYING is less efficient than PERFORM n TIMES with the user writing
            the ADD statements to emulate the VARYING option.
         9. Use of the SEARCH verb is more efficient in scanning tables especially if the
            SEARCH ALL option is used.

17.2.2.2. Input/Output
         1. DISPLAY and ACCEPT are less efficient than writing to a printer file or reading from a
            card-reader file.
         2. Multi-key Indexed files should use the RESERVE clause to allow as many buffer
            areas as possible for processing. If a RESERVE clause is specified, the COBOL
            compiler causes the use of (4 + n + a) buffers at run time where n = integer - 1 of
            the RESERVE clause and a = number of alternate keys. When no RESERVE clause
            is stated, the number of buffers will be (5 + a). Thus, when there are no alternate
            keys, the minimum number of buffers allowed is 5. The compiler-generated number
            of buffers can be altered by means of the Define File Processor (see 20.2).
         3. Block size for a Multi-Key Indexed file is determined by the compiler in the following
            manner. In the absence of a BLOCK clause in the file description entry, the compiler
            generates a block size which is the larger of a. and b. which follow, rounded up to a
            multiple of 448 words.
             a.   200*(kl + 1 + x) + 8
                  where kl = largest key length in words; x = 1 if duplicate keys are allowed,
                  otherwise x = 0.
             b. 10*(mrl + 2 + ndk) + 6
                  where mrl = maximum record length in words; ndk = number of keys with
                  duplicates.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                    17ΓÇô3
Optimization




            This block size is the minimum the COBOL compiler will allow, even in the case
            where a BLOCK clause is specified. If a BLOCK CONTAINS integerΓÇô2
            CHARACTERS clause is specified, the COBOL compiler rounds integerΓÇô2 (ASCII)
            characters up to a number of words and then rounds up again to a multiple of 448
            words. This computed block size must be at least as large as the minimum
            acceptable block size. If a BLOCK CONTAINS integerΓÇô2 RECORDS clause is
            specified, the compiler calculates the block size, rounded up to a multiple of 448
            words, as:
                 integerΓÇô2 * (mrl + 2 + ndk) + 6
            This computed block size is checked against the minimum acceptable block size. In
            any case, block size should be sufficient to allow for at least 10 maximum length
            records or 200 maximum length keys. The compiler-generated block size can be
            altered by means of the Define File Processor (see 20.2).
        4. When a Multi-Key Indexed file is created and integer-1 of the BLOCK clause is
           specified, the ratio of integer-1 divided by integer-2 of the BLOCK clause indicates
           the portion of each data block and index block which is filled. The remaining portion
           of the block (called the block loading factor when expressed in words) is then
           available for insertion of additional records in the file within the range of keys
           originally put into that block. The compiler-generated block loading factor can be
           altered by use of the Define File Processor (see 20.2). If a significant amount of
           activity on the file involves deletions or insertions of records, the portion of reserved
           space in each block should be higher at file creation time than if few deletions or
           insertions are anticipated.
        5. Initial creation of a Multi-Key Indexed file is slightly faster if the access mode is
           sequential compared to the random or dynamic access modes. This does, however,
           impose the restriction that the prime record keys must be presented in an ascending
           sequence.
        6. Blocksize for a RELATIVE DISC file is determined in the following manner:
               MINBUF = MRL + NCW + 2*(PF-1)+1

            where:
               MRL = maximum record length in words,
               NCW = number of control words per record = (MRL+2046)/2047
               PF = prepping factor (default is 112)

            If the resulting MINBUF is less than 1792 words (in other words, 1 track), then 1792
            will be assumed.

            Through the use of the Define File Processor, the default of 1792 can be overridden.
            A DFP specified blocksize, in terms of characters, will be used if it exceeds the
            MINBUF as calculated above. A DFP specified blocksize in terms of records, will
            cause a multiple of MINBUF to be used. DFP may also be used to alter PF in the
            MINBUF calculation (see 20.2).

        7. Blocksize for a SEQUENTIAL DISC file is always rounded up to a multiple of the
           prepping factor. The default prepping factor is 112, but it may be increased to 224,
           448, 896, or 1792 by means of the Define File Processor (see 20.2).



17ΓÇô4                                                                                7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                     Optimization




17.2.2.3. Sort
         1. Allows perform a disk sort (in other words, assign three or more equally sized
            scratch files).
         2. Perform an extended mode sort versus a basic mode sort. Assign the file R$CORE
            with a maximumn reserve of at least 211 granules. This size represents a sort
            memory size in thousands of words. The larger the size generally implies a more
            efficient sort.

17.2.2.4. Data Alignment and Data Types
         1. Conversion from one data format to another is costly. Consistent data descriptions
            will generally result in faster execution.
         2. For indexing or subscripting, better code is generated if all the dimensions have
            integral word sizes; in other words, all the items with OCCURS clauses have sizes
            which are an integral multiple of 4 ASCII bytes.
         3. Data should be aligned as much as possible to word boundaries.
         4. Alphanumeric moves and compares are most efficient if both operands start and end
            on the word boundary. Equal start byte moves are more efficient than unequal start
            byte moves.
         5. Alphanumeric moves and compares of unequal length operands are more costly than
            equal length moves of similar length. An exception to this rule is when the longer
            operand is longer by 3 words or more.
         6. Certain operations on decimal fields are done more efficiently if the ΓÇ£SΓÇ¥ is omitted.
            For example, a DISPLAY data item which is defined with an operational sign would
            perhaps require more elaborate handling to convert it to a binary format.

17.2.2.5. Execution of Extended Instruction Set (EIS) Instruction
         Execution speed generally can be increased by using the EIS instructions generated by
         the compilier. See 2.4.1.2.4 for the steps necessary to cause EIS instructions to be
         generated.

17.2.2.6. Generation of Inline Code
         When EIS instructions are not generated the following recommendation will improve
         code efficiency:
         1. For small fields (1 ΓÇô 4 ASCII bytes or 1 ΓÇô 36 bits) which are frequently referenced in
            arithmetic move and compare statements, the best inline code is generated when
            the fields are j-factorable; in other words, allocated in one whole word, a physical
            half-word, or a physical quarter-word. Avoid ASCII fields of 3 bytes.
         2. Inline code will be generated for the following functions:
             a.   Alphanumeric moves when the sending and receiving fields have equal start
                  bytes and size of receiver is less than 512 bytes in length; if both sender and
                  receiver start at byte 0 there is no restriction on length.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                   17ΓÇô5
Optimization




           b. All comparisons where both fields have equal start bytes, are less than 512
              bytes in length, and are equal in length, or if after scaling and padding two items
              of different lengths are less than two words in length.
           c.   ASCII to binary conversion for 1 ΓÇô 4 bytes, unsigned.
           d. Binary to ASCII conversions for 1 ΓÇô 6 bytes unsigned.
           e. Moving 1 or 2 characters ASCII to any alphanumeric field.

17.2.2.7. Programmer-Controlled Optimization
        1. Optimization regions should be determined. For smaller programs this region could
           be the entire Procedure Division. For larger programs the optimization regions
           should be high-use areas. A frequency analysis of programs can be made by using
           the 7 option in the Extra Options field of the @ACOB statement, the USE FOR
           DEBUGGING syntax, and the object listing of the program. (See 17.3.)
        2. When the optimization regions are determined the following techniques can be
           applied.
           a.   For cases where inline code is not being generated, operands could possibly be
                changed so that inline code is generated.
           b. Moves of equal size fields with different starting bytes, which cannot be
              changed to generate inline code, could be changed to several moves of smaller
              parts of the original fields through use of REDEFINES clause, redefining the
              fields to j-factorable parts of the receiving field.
           c.   Inefficient conversions and scalings could be eliminated.
           d. The COBOL algorithms could be changed, for example, the most likely pattern in
              a complex IF statement should be the first comparison made.

17.2.3. Compilation Speed
        The following items have a direct bearing on compiler speed:
        1. Using FILLER instead of named but unreferenced fields is more efficient.
        2. Reducing the number of nonunique names and qualified references will increase
           compilation speed. Avoid including unnecessary qualification.
        3. CORRESPONDING ADD, SUBTRACT, and MOVE statements require more time to
           compile than do the explicit simple MOVE, ADD, or SUBTRACT statements.
        4. Large numbers of user names (procedural and data) are processed more efficiently if
           they are formed by appending a varying prefix or suffix to a constant.
        5. Fieldata source programs are converted to ASCII upon input to the compiler.




17ΓÇô6                                                                              7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                                     Optimization




17.3. Frequency Table Generation
         Frequency table generation allows COBOL programmers to accumulate a frequency
         analysis of their program while running live data. This feature is invoked via the 7 option
         in the Extra Options field of the @ACOB statement and requires the USE FOR
         DEBUGGING syntax.

         When a COBOL program is compiled with the 7 option in the Extra Options field, all
         procedures that are presently being debugged, via USE FOR DEBUGGING, will
         automatically be tabled for frequency analysis. Each time the program enters one of
         these tabled procedures, its frequency count is incremented by one. Upon reaching
         STOP RUN this frequency information is tabulated for each procedure referenced, sorted
         in frequency order, and printed in a report.

         In order to perform such a frequency analysis, for example, on a COBOL run unit
         consisting of one main program named MAIN, and two subprograms named SUB1 and
         SUB2, the three COBOL programs MAIN, SUB1, and SUB2 must be changed to add the
         following syntax:
         1.   WITH DEBUGGING MODE clause on the SOURCE-COMPUTER paragraph.

         2.   USE FOR DEBUGGING ON ALL PROCEDURES in the DECLARATIVES.

         Recompile each program with the 7 option in the Extra Options field of the @ACOB
         statement. When mapped and executed, the frequency table will be printed upon
         detection of a STOP RUN. The @XQT statement with D option will inhibit the building of
         DEBUGΓÇôITEM but will still do the frequency count.

         This feature should identify high-use sections of code in programs while running with live
         data. Those high-use sections identified are then candidates for examination and
         optimization.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                   17ΓÇô7
Optimization

Section 18
System Interface


18.1. Processor Call Statement
         The @ACOB processor call statement conforms to the standard format for calling an OS
         2200 processor. See OS 2200 Executive System Software Executive Control Language
         (ECL) Operations and Programming Reference Manual.

         The option letters that are unique to the ASCII COBOL compiler are documented in the
         following section. The ASCII COBOL compiler uses the Source Input Routine to control
         the input and output of the source language elements. (See OS 2200 System Service
         Routines Library (SYSLIB) Programming Reference Manual.)

18.1.1. General Format
            @ACOB,options SI,RO,SO,EO


18.1.2. General Rules
         1. Options specifies the options consisting of letters. See Table 18-1 for a description
            of the allowable options.
         2. SI (Source Input) specifies the program file and symbolic element name of the
            source language to be processed. (See OS 2200 Executive System, Software
            Executive Control Language (ECL) Operations and Programming Reference Manual.)
         3. RO (Relocatable Output) specifies the program file and element name where the
            relocatable element will be placed. For a segmented program, this specifies the
            program file and element name given to the symbolic MAP and the main Procedure
            Division (Sections 0ΓÇô49) relocatable element.
         4. SO (Source Output) specifies the program file and element name given to the
            updated source language element. (See OS 2200 Executive System, Software
            Executive Control Language (ECL) Operations and Programming Reference Manual.)
         5. EO (Extra Options) specifies the extra options consisting of a string of numbers or
            letters. See Table 18ΓÇô2 for a description of the allowable options.

18.2. XQT Options
        The @XQT statement initiates the execution of a program that is in absolute element
        format. (See Series 2200 Executive System, EXEC Programmer Reference (7830 9945))

        The option letters that are unique to ASCII COBOL are documented here.

18.2.1. General Format

        See Table 18-3 for a description of the allowable options.


                                    Table 18-3. @XQT Options


          Option                                     Description

                    operate as they do in batch mode. (See 2.6.4 and 2.6.6.)

18.3. Auto-Flagging Compiler
         The symbolic release tape contains two versions of the ASCII COBOL compiler. One
         version is the normal ASCII COBOL compiler as released prior to level 5R2CY. The other
         compiler is the flagging compiler. The normal compiler has full capabilities of all parts of
         ASCII COBOL and all options work the same as before. The flagging compiler diagnoses
         all non-standard uses of COBOL by DEFAULT, and can be turned off by option. In
         addition, some options and features of ASCII COBOL have been disabled or modified.

         The flagging compiler is intended for sites that want to use the basic COBOL
         environment or write programs that comply with the American National Standards
         Institute COBOL. Therefore, use careful judgment when you install the flagging
         compiler if your site previously used the normal compiler.

         The following EXTRA OPTIONS have been DISABLED:
          C     EBCDIC allocation and alignment rules outside the FILE SECTION are not used.
          E     Procedures in the 1968 American National Standard standard format may not be
                used to satisfy a COPY.
          T     Forcing numeric expressions and COMPUTE statements to use floating point for
                intermediate results is not possible.

         The flagging compiler has the following STANDARD OPTION set:
          M     ALL MONITOR statements are ignored.


         The flagging compiler has the following EXTRA OPTIONS set:
          D     HIGHΓÇôVALUES is represented internally by the octal value 0377 instead of 0177.
          M     Lowercase letters are NOT folded to uppercase letters.
          N     Data items with USAGE COMP or COMPΓÇô4 are treated as though DISP or DISPΓÇô1
                were specified. (See the following special note on effects of using this option
                with the flagging compiler).
          O     The source input file is searched before COB$PF when looking for a procedure to
                satisfy a COPY without the optional library name specified.
          R     All violations of American National Standard COBOL X3.23.1974 are diagnosed.
                (See the following special note on effects of using this option with the flagging
                compiler).
          V     All nonnumeric literals must be delimited by quotation marks rather than
                apostrophes. (See the following special note on effects of using this option with
                the flagging compiler).




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                   18ΓÇô7
System Interface




        When used with the flagging compiler, the following EXTRA OPTIONS are MODIFIED:
         N    Using the N extra option with the flagging compiler causes the NORMAL meaning
              to the USAGEs COMP and COMPΓÇô4. (Reverse of normal).
         R    Using the R extra option with the flagging compiler disables flagging, requires
              apostrophes for nonnumeric literals, and folds lowercase letters to uppercase
              letters except in nonnumeric literals. (Unsets the R, V, and M extra options.
              Reverse of normal).
         V    Using the V extra option with the flagging compiler requires that apostrophes be
              used to delimit nonnumeric literals. (Reverse of normal).


        In addition to the options changes, the segmentation feature has been disabled and all
        compilations produce one relocatable element (two relocatables for subprograms). In
        other words, all segmentation directives to the compiler are ignored.

        A special note about using the R and V EXTRA OPTIONS together:

        Using the R and V EXTRA OPTIONS together with the flagging compiler disables the
        flagging and folds lowercase letters to uppercase letters. However, nonnumeric literals
        must be delimited by quotation marks. (In other words, unsets the EXTRA OPTIONS R
        and M, but not V).

        Using the N and R EXTRA OPTIONS with the flagging compiler makes the flagging
        compiler act as though it is a normal compiler, with the exception of the feature and
        options that have been disabled, using 0377 instead of 0177 for HIGHΓÇôVALUES, and the
        searching of the source input file before COB$PF to satisfy a COPY without the optional
        library name specified.

18.5. COPY Procedures
18.5.1. Library Preparation
        To prepare an ASCII COBOL source library, source images are processed by the
        Procedure Definition Processor (@PDP). The PDP output produces an ASCII COBOL
        library, which can be accessed by COBOL programs via the COPY statement.

        Several procedures (text items) may be grouped together in one element, but each
        separate text-name must appear in the label field of a PROC statement.

        The format for a text item input to PDP is:
             text-name PROC

                 (COBOL statements to be copied)

              END

        The parameter text-name may consist only of the characters ΓÇ£AΓÇ¥ through ΓÇ£ZΓÇ¥, ΓÇ£0ΓÇ¥
        through ΓÇ£9ΓÇ¥, and ΓÇ£-ΓÇ¥ except that the ΓÇ£-ΓÇ¥ may not appear as the first or last character.
        The parameter text-name must begin in column 1 of the source image and END must
        begin in column 2. Library text must conform to the rules for ASCII COBOL reference
        format.

18.5.2. Library Search Algorithm
        The various COPY statements in the source program can reference text from more than
        one library. Only the library-name specified is searched to satisfy the COPY request.

        When the library-name is not specified, the text can be found in any of the following
        libraries:

        SI
              Source Input File.

        COB$PF
              A user-defined file with the attached name COB$PF that the compiler references to
              satisfy COPY requests. If this file is not assigned, the compiler attempts to
              dynamically assign it. If COB$PF is dynamically assigned, it will not be freed at the
              end of compilation. If a file with the attached name COB$PF is not present, the
              search of this file is skipped.

        SYS$LIB$*PROC$
              A file created and maintained by COMUS and SOLAR to contain system procedures
              that the compiler references to satisfy COPY requests. If this file is not assigned,
              the compiler dynamically assigns it. If it is dynamically assigned, it will not be freed
              at the end of compilation. If SYS$LIB$*PROC$ is not present, the search of this file
              is skipped.




18ΓÇô12                                                                                 7830 7709ΓÇô002
                                                                               System Interface




         SYS$*RLIB$
             A file built during a system generation run.

         Table 18-6 specifies the library search order when attempting to satisfy COPY requests.

18.6.4. Definition of Cross Reference and Allocation Listings
        The following describes the usage of the cross reference and allocation listings.

        (1) Title of page

        (2) NAME
            List of user names which have been defined within the program. Use of the R
            option is for cross reference in alphabetic order; the D option is for allocation listings
            only.

        (3) DEFN
            The internal line number at which the data item is defined.

        (4) TYPE
            Type of item; in other words, data, section, file, etc.

        (5) USAGE
            Type of usage; in other words, alphanumeric, numeric, or binary.

        (6) DIM
            Dimension. A zero in the dimension field indicates nondimensioned; a number
            greater than zero indicates the number of dimensions.

        (7) SIZE
            Size in bytes for character data; size in bits for binary data.

        (8) SB
            Starting bit. (The convention is left to right with the zero bit being the leftmost bit.)

        (9) ADDRESS
            Relative address within the area defined under FILE NAME.

        (10) FILE NAME
            The file name, working storage area, etc., described in the program.

        (11) REFS**
            All source lines containing reference to this location, excluding the originally defined
            location DEFN.

        (12) Starred references mean that the contents of dataΓÇônames are changed by this
             reference. An example would be the object of a MOVE.

        Note: If a COPY statement is used, there will be two sets of line numbers listed on the
        left side of the source listing. In this case, DEFN refers to the internal line number listed
        on the leftmost side of the source listing.

18.7. Interprogram Communication Considerations
18.7.1. CALL Identifier
         Usage of the CALL identifier format of the CALL statement requires some extra work at
         program collection time. The addresses of all the potential called programs, to be
         referenced by identifier, must be made available to the called program interface routine.
         This is accomplished by including a relocatable element (C$S333) in the collection. This
         table element contains all necessary information concerning potential called programs
         referenced by the identifier. If identifier references a called program name not found in
         the C$S333 element, the calling program terminates in error.

         The C$S333 is a @MASM symbolic element which is found in the @ACOB run-time
         library file. The user must reassemble this element with MASM adding the list of
         subroutines to be referenced by CALL identifier to the source. The MASM-created
         relocatable C$S333 is collected with the program.

         The subroutines can be collected in common banks, program banks, or segments.

         Each subroutine referenced by using the CALL identifier format of the CALL statement
         must be specified in the source of C$S333 using the following format:
           CREATE subroutine entry-point-name,n

         where n is zero (0), an unsigned positive integer or is not specified. The intent of the
         CREATE statement is to generate two external references for the subroutine
         entry-point-name, one for the I-bank entry-point-name and the other for the D-bank C$B
         entry-point-name. If n is specified as zero or is not specified, two external references are
         generated. If only an I-bank external reference is required, the D-bank external reference
         can be omitted by specifying n as an unsigned positive integer. Note that the D-bank
         external reference is required if the ΓÇ£MEMORY 3 MODULESΓÇ¥ clause is used in the
         called program and that the absence of the D-bank external reference during collection
         can cause the Collector to issue the following error message:
           *ERROR: entry point C$Bentry-point-name referenced from element element-name is
                   undefined name

         The current maximum number of external references allowed in this element is 1024 as
         specified in the OS 2200 Data Structures Programming Reference Manual.

System Interface




        An example of a MASM of C$S333 and a collection using that relocatable follows:
          @MASM,SE SYS$LIB$*ACOB. C$S333,RBFILE.C$S333
          -40
                   CREATE 'SUBPROGRAM1'
                   CREATE 'SUB3'
                   CREATE 'WRITER'
                   CREATE 'SUN-BREAK'
           @EOF

          @MAP   ,PROGRAM
          IN   MAIN
          IN   RBFILE.C$S333
          LIB SUBPGMFILE.
          LIB SYS$LIB$*ACOB.
          END

        Note: C$S333 symbolics are found in the ASCII COBOL product file. In this example:
        SYS$LIB$*ACOB.

        An alternative to this C$S333 method is to place the identifier subprogram I-bank
        entry-point-names in a DEF list (Collector directive). For example:

          @MAP   ,PROGRAM
          IN   MAIN
          LIB SUBPGMFILE.
          DEF SUBPROGRAM1,SUB3,WRITER,SUN-BREAK
          LIB SYS$LIB$*ACOB.

        If the ΓÇ£MEMORY 3 MODULESΓÇ¥ clause was used to compile the called programs,
        another DEF defining the D-bank entry-points must be included. For example:

          @MAP   ,PROGRAM
          IN   MAIN
          LIB SUBPGMFILE.
          DEF SUBPROGRAMS,SUB3,WRITER,SUN-BREAK
          DEF C$BSUBPROGRAM1,C$BSUB3,C$BWRITER,C$BSUN-BREAK
          LIB SYS$LIB$*ACOB.

        All called programs must be included in the MAP with a DEF of the I-bank entry-points
        and, if the MEMORY clause is used, a DEF of the D-bank entry-points. This means that
        the called programs cannot be in a program bank or common bank when using this
        method. The C$S333 method allows usage of banked called programs. When using the
        DEF list approach, if a particular called program is not found in the C$S333 list, the MAP
        DEF directives will be searched.

18.7.2. ASCII COBOL Programs Calling NonΓÇôCOBOL Programs
18.7.2.1. Preserving the COBOL Environment
         The non-COBOL program being called must preserve the COBOL programΓÇÖs
         environment. That is, the called program must save and restore those registers which
         COBOL programs assume to be nonvolatile (normally the volatile registers are A0
         through A5 and R1 through R3), should not alter interrupt trap locations set and used by
         ASCII COBOL, must not get its own dynamic storage areas, must not change the
         processor state word, and must not initiate random processing cycles except through
         the ASCII COBOL asynchronous processing facility, etc.

18.7.2.2. ENTER MASM Calling Sequence
         When ENTER MASM is specified, the calling sequence will be:

             $(1).
                     L,U   A0,parameters
                     LXI,U X11,BDICALL$ + subpgm
                     IBJ$  X11,subpgm
             $(8).
             parameters
                 +          C$Bsubpgm,n
                 +          Word 1 of parameterΓÇô1
                 +          Word 2 of parameterΓÇô1
                 .
                 .
                 .
                 +          Word 1 of parameterΓÇôn
                 +          Word 2 of parameterΓÇôn
             $(1).

         where:

         subpgm
              is the I-bank entry-point.

         C$Bsubpgm
              is the reference to an entry-point in the called programΓÇÖs D-bank and is the name
              derived from the I-bank entry-point. This allows called programs to utilize based
              D-bank references and is the technique used to pass the called programΓÇÖs D-bank
              from the calling bank to the called program common bank.
              C$Bsubpgm is derived from the entry-point. If the entry-point is nine or fewer
              characters in length, the entire entry-point is appended to C$B. If the entry-point is
              greater than nine characters, the first three and last six characters are appended to
              C$B.

         n
              is a value equal to twice the number of operands contained in the USING phrase of
              the ENTER statement. If the USING phrase of the ENTER statement is not
              specified, only the LXI,U and IBJ$ instructions are generated.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                  18ΓÇô21
System Interface




          Two words will be generated for each operand contained in the USING phrase of the
          ENTER statement. For a description of the parameter formats, see 18.7.2.4. For a
          description of the number and types of parameters which may be passed to MASM, see
          12.4.4.

18.7.2.3. ENTER ASM Calling Sequence
          When ENTER ASM is specified, the calling sequence will be:

              LMJ          X11,subpgm
              +        2*n
              +        Word 1 of parameter-1
              +        Word 2 of parameter-1
                        .
                        .
                        .
              +        Word 1 of parameter-n
              +        Word 2 of parameter-n
              Next instruction

          where:

          subpgm
               is the I-bank entry-point.

          n
               contains a value equal to the number of operands contained in the USING phrase of
               the ENTER statement. If the USING phrase of the ENTER statement is not
               specified, only the LMJ instruction is generated.

          Two words will be generated for each operand contained in the USING phrase of the
          ENTER statement. For a description of the parameter formats, see 18.7.2.4. For a
          description of the number and types of parameters which may be passed to ASM, see
          12.4.4.

18.7.2.4. Parameter Format for MASM and ASM
          Two words are generated for each operand contained in the USING phrase of the ENTER
          statement. These two words have the following format:

    C D                      F              H                          I

    0 1 2           5 6           11 12         17 18                                        35

    A G        B J           K              E                          L
    0 1         4 5 6             11 12         17 18                                        35

                                         synchronized.
            D             1       1      If = 1 this item is a constant.

18.7.2.4.1. Evaluation of Subscripted Arguments

        For either array-sync or non-array-sync table elements, the operand address can be
        determined by examining the F, H and I fields of the first word of the parameter. These
        fields are not maintained dynamically, however, the H field may reference an X-register
        that contains:
            H1 = unnormalized bit offset
            H2 = word offset

        To locate the array element in question, multiply the F field value by either 9 to convert
        to bits unless MAJOR USE (M$USE) is 3 in which case it is bits already. Add this to the
        unnormalized bit offset (H1 of the X-register) and convert the result to words and bits by
        dividing by 36. Add the words just calculated to the sum of the I field value and the
        word offset (H2 of the X-register). This gives the array element word address while the
        remainder (bit count resulting from the division by 36) gives the start bit of the element
        within that word.

18.7.2.4.2. Evaluation of Arguments Containing an ODO Clause

        When an item containing an ODO clause is used as an argument the maximum length of
        the item is passed in field L since this length is created at compile time and is not altered
        dynamically at run time.

18.7.2.5. ENTER PL1 Calling Sequence
         When ENTER PL1 "ROUTINENAME" USING dn1 is specified, it will cause the following code
         sequence to be generated:
           $(1).
                    L,U      A0,$(8)                     . parameter list address
                    LXI,U    A0,1                        . number of parameters
                    LMJ      X11,C$M706                  . PL1 prologue
                    LXI,U    X11,BDICALL$+ROUTINENAME
                    IBJ$     X11,ROUTINENAME
           $(8)     +        dn1
           $(1)     LMJ      X11,C$M707                  . PL1 epilogue


         where dn1 is an elementary or group item with one of the following COBOL usages:

            (1)    USAGE IS DISPLAY,
            (2)    USAGE IS COMPUTATIONAL (4 or 8 bytes in length starting on a word boundary),
            (3)    USAGE IS COMPUTATIONALΓÇô1,
            (4)    USAGE IS COMPUTATIONALΓÇô2,
            (5)    Exact Binary.


         The corresponding allowable PL1 data types are as follows:

            (1)    CHARACTER (nonvarying),
            (2)    BINARY FIXED, DECIMAL FIXED,
            (3)    DECIMAL FLOAT (8),
            (4)    DECIMAL FLOAT (16),
            (5)    BIT.

         If a COBOL main program passes an array or a structure as an argument to a PL/I
         subprogram, care must be taken in how the parameter is declared in the PL/I
         subprogram. PL/I requires aggregate descriptors whereas COBOL does not generate
         them. COBOL does create string descriptors for arguments passed to PL/I
         subprograms. However, for arrays and structures, the length used in the descriptor is
         the total length of the array or structure. Therefore, in the PL/I subprogram, the
         parameter must be declared as a character string with the array or structure defined in
         the parameter so that the elements of the array or the members of the structure can be
         referenced.




7830 7709ΓÇô002                                                                                     18ΓÇô25
System Interface




        Example:
        COBOL main program:
          01     NUMBER-BUFFER USAGE DISPLAY.
                 02 NUMBER-ARRAY OCCURS 5 PIC X(12).
                     ENTER PL1 'ACOB' USING NUMBER-BUFFER.

        PL/I subprogram:
          DCL ARRAY CHARACTER (60);
          DCL ARRAY1 (5) PIC '(12)X' DEFINED (ARRAY);


18.7.2.6. ENTER FTN Calling Sequence
        When ENTER FTN "ROUTINENAME" USING dn1 is specified, it will cause the following code
        sequence to be generated:

          $(1).
                   L,U      A0,$(8)                    . parameter list address
                   LXI,U    A0,1                       . number of parameters
                   LMJ      X11,C$M708                 . FTN prologue
                   LXI,U    X11,BDICALL$+ROUTINENAME
                   IBJ$     X11,ROUTINENAME
          $(8)     +        dn1
          $(1)     LMJ      X11,C$M709                 . FTN epilogue

        where dn1 is an elementary item with one of the following COBOL usages:

            (1)     USAGE IS DISPLAY,
            (2)     USAGE IS COMPUTATIONAL (4 bytes in length starting on a word boundary),
            (3)     USAGE IS COMPUTATIONALΓÇô1,
            (4)     USAGE IS COMPUTATIONALΓÇô2.

        The parameter dn1 may also be a COBOL paragraph-name.

        The corresponding allowable FTN data types are as follows:

            (1)     CHARACTER,
            (2)     INTEGER,
            (3)     REAL,
            (4)     DOUBLE PRECISION.

        When dn1 is a group item, the corresponding FTN data type may be anything but
        CHARACTER.
